summary: Solar facilities may not be built on agricultural-district land with the best (class A) soils, and on class B or C soils they are limited to 10 percent of the parcel or 20 acres, whichever is less, unless a county special permit is granted (with Land Use Commission approval over 15 acres) and the area is offered for farming at reduced rent and bonded for decommissioning. Wind facilities are a permitted use in the agricultural district if compatible with agriculture.
amendments_note: HRS 205-4.5 history shows am. L 2024, c 182 (overnight camps) and am. L 2025, c 255 (landfill siting); HRS 205-2 history shows am. L 2025, c 255. I read both session laws (SLH2024_Act182.pdf, SLH2025_Act255.pdf on data.capitol.hawaii.gov): neither changes the solar or wind provisions.
draft_note: Read HRS 205-4.5(a) paras (15), (20), (21) and HRS 205-2(d)(6),(8) on data.capitol.hawaii.gov (HRS_0205-0004_0005.htm, HRS_0205-0002.htm). The soil class limits come from the land study bureau ratings named in the statute.
review_note: Read HRS 205-4.5(a) intro, (15), (20), (21) (https://data.capitol.hawaii.gov/hrscurrent/Vol04_Ch0201-0257/HRS0205/HRS_0205-0004_0005.htm) and 205-2(d)(4),(6),(8) (HRS_0205-0002.htm), 2026-10-09. Matches: (20) solar not permitted on class A; on class B or C limited to 10 percent of the parcel or 20 acres, whichever is lesser, unless a 205-6 special use permit is granted; (21) a special-permit facility on B or C land must offer the area for compatible agriculture at a lease rate at least 50 percent below fair market rent, show decommissioning financial security, and be decommissioned within 12 months; 205-6(d) adds LUC approval over 15 acres; (15) wind facilities are a permitted use if compatible with agriculture. Amendments: 205-4.5 history ends am L 2024, c 182, s2 and am L 2025, c 255, s3; 205-2 ends am L 2025, c 255, s2; the text read is the current text including those acts, and the solar and wind provisions read as summarized. I did not open the session laws themselves. Note for the drafter (not a contradiction): the summary describes wind (205-4.5(a)(15)) but technology is solar only and the citation omits (a)(15); either drop the wind sentence or cite it.

summary: Counties decide siting of wind and solar through zoning and county planning commission special permits; there is no state siting board. The state Land Use Commission must also approve a special permit for land over 15 acres in the agricultural district.
amendments_note: HRS 205-6 history shows am. L 2025, c 236, s17 (Act 236, a biosecurity act that renames agencies; not a siting change). No other change after 2021 shown on data.capitol.hawaii.gov as of 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Read HRS 205-6 on data.capitol.hawaii.gov (the www.capitol.hawaii.gov copy returned HTTP 403 on 2026-10-09). Subsection (c)/(d): special permits for land over 15 acres or on important agricultural lands need Land Use Commission approval. Local primacy is the default under county zoning; no state statute assigns siting of utility-scale wind or solar to a state body. Public-land leases (HRS 171-95.3) not read.
review_note: Read HRS 205-6 (https://data.capitol.hawaii.gov/hrscurrent/Vol04_Ch0201-0257/HRS0205/HRS_0205-0006.htm), 205-2 (HRS_0205-0002.htm) and 205-4.5 (HRS_0205-0004_0005.htm) on data.capitol.hawaii.gov, 2026-10-09. 205-6(a),(c): the county planning commission grants special permits for unusual uses in agricultural and rural districts; 205-6(d): permits for land over fifteen acres (or designated important agricultural lands) need Land Use Commission approval. Checked for a state siting process: HRS chapter 201N (Renewable Energy Facility Siting Process) shows REPEALED, L 2016, c 27, s6, so no state siting body remains. local_government, blank state_body and threshold fit. Amendments: 205-6 history ends am L 2025, c 236, s17; the current text read names the department of agriculture and biosecurity (a rename) and nothing in (a) to (e) bears on wind or solar siting. Minor: the 15-acre LUC step also applies to rural districts and to important agricultural lands of any size; the summary is not wrong, only narrower.

summary: For a facility that needs a state certificate (25 MW or more, or storage of 25 MWh or more), failing city, county or airport zoning does not stop the Commission from issuing it, and once it issues no city, county or regulatory agency may require any further approval, permit or license for construction.
amendments_note: 476A.5 history: 2024 Iowa Acts ch. 1170, s369 (agency rename) only. 476A.8 shows only [C77, 79, 81, s476A.8], no later amendment. Per the Iowa Code 2026 PDF on legis.iowa.gov (printed 2025-12-09); the 2026 session table of Code sections amended (legis.iowa.gov/law/statutory/acts/amended?year=2026), read 2026-10-09, lists no change to chapter 476A.
draft_note: Corrects the 2026-10-09 draft after review: removed battery_storage:25 from threshold_mw (476A.1(5) sets storage at 25 megawatt hours, not MW) and put the 25 MWh storage trigger in the summary; amendments_note no longer says 476A.8 was amended in 2024 (its history shows no amendment since the 1981 Code), which I confirmed. Summary now also names airport zoning and regulatory agencies, as the text does. Read 2026-10-09 in https://www.legis.iowa.gov/docs/code/476A.pdf: 476A.5(3) ('The failure of a facility to meet zoning requirements established pursuant to chapters 329, 335 and 414 shall not preclude the commission from issuing the certificate') and 476A.8 ('a regulatory agency, city or county shall not require any further approval, permit or license for the construction of the facility'), and 476A.1(5).
review_note: Read 2026-10-09 https://www.legis.iowa.gov/docs/code/476A.pdf (Iowa Code 2026). 476A.5(3): zoning authorities may state whether the facility meets city, county and airport zoning requirements, and failure to meet zoning under chapters 329, 335 and 414 shall not preclude the commission from issuing the certificate, superseding those chapters to that extent. 476A.8: upon issuance of a certificate, notwithstanding any provision of law except statutory requirements protecting employees engaged in construction, a regulatory agency, city or county shall not require any further approval, permit or license for the construction of the facility. Summary matches (it leaves out the worker-protection exception, which is an omission, not an error). 476A.1(5) gives the 25 MW and 25 MWh triggers; threshold_mw solar:25;wind:25 matches and storage is correctly kept out of the MW field. who_decides state_board and state_body Iowa Utilities Commission (476A.1(4)) correct. Amendments: 476A.5 history is [C77, 79, 81] and 2024 Acts ch 1170 s369 only; 476A.8 shows only [C77, 79, 81, s476A.8]. The 2026 Code sections amended table (legis.iowa.gov/law/statutory/acts/amended?year=2026) lists no chapter 476A section. No change after June 2024 affects the row.

summary: A generating plant or group of plants at a single site totaling 25 MW or more, or an electric storage unit of 25 MWh or more, needs a certificate of public convenience, use and necessity from the Iowa Utilities Commission; smaller facilities need no Commission certificate and are left to county and city zoning.
amendments_note: 476A.1 history ends 2024 Iowa Acts ch. 1108, s4 (adds electric storage units of 25 MWh or more to the facility definition) and ch. 1170, s369 (Utilities Board renamed Utilities Commission), per the Iowa Code 2026 PDF on legis.iowa.gov (printed 2025-12-09). The 2026 session table of Code sections amended (legis.iowa.gov/law/statutory/acts/amended?year=2026), read 2026-10-09, lists no change to chapter 476A.
draft_note: Corrects the 2026-10-09 draft after review: removed battery_storage:25 from threshold_mw because 476A.1(5) sets the storage trigger at twenty-five or more megawatt hours, an energy figure, not MW; the 25 MWh storage trigger is kept in the summary. Replaced the unchecked note on 2026 HF 2580 with a check of the 2026 Code sections amended table. Reviewer agreed on everything else and I agree with the reviewer. Read 2026-10-09: Iowa Code 2026 chapter 476A PDF (https://www.legis.iowa.gov/docs/code/476A.pdf), 476A.1(4) and (5), 476A.2(1) ('a person shall not commence to construct a facility ... unless a certificate for the facility has been issued by the commission'). The local-zoning half of hybrid rests on chapters 335 (county) and 414 (city) zoning applying where no certificate preempts them (476A.5(3)); those chapters were not read for this row. Not checked: Mathis v. Palo Alto Wind (Iowa 2021), which LBNL says treats separately connected turbines as separate facilities.
review_note: Read 2026-10-09 the Iowa Code 2026 chapter 476A PDF at https://www.legis.iowa.gov/docs/code/476A.pdf (printed Dec 09 2025). 476A.1(5) defines facility as any generating plant, electric storage unit or combination at a single site with total capacity of twenty-five or more megawatts for plants or twenty-five or more megawatt hours for storage units; 476A.1(4) commission means the utilities commission; 476A.2(1) a person shall not commence to construct a facility unless a certificate has been issued by the commission; 476A.1(2) the certificate is one of public convenience, use and necessity. threshold_mw solar:25;wind:25 matches, and leaving storage out of threshold_mw is right because the storage trigger is in MWh, which the summary states. Local half of hybrid: county zoning power in Iowa Code 335.3(1) (location and use of buildings, structures and land) and city zoning in chapter 414, read at https://www.legis.iowa.gov/docs/code/335.pdf and /414.pdf; neither mentions wind or solar, and 476A.5(3) supersedes them only for certificated facilities, so smaller facilities fall under local zoning by inference from these general grants. Citation correct. Amendments: 476A.1 history ends 2024 Acts ch 1108 s4 and ch 1170 s369, 476A.2 ends 2024 Acts ch 1170 s369, as the note says. The 2026 Code sections amended table (https://www.legis.iowa.gov/law/statutory/acts/amended?year=2026), read 2026-10-09, lists no 476A section; 2026 HF 2799 adds 476.10C and 476.59 (load forecasting and transmission planning per its title), not siting. Nothing after June 2024 beyond the 2024 acts changes the row.

state_body: Idaho Transportation Department, Division of Aeronautics
summary: A new wind energy conversion system (5 or more turbines at least 50 feet tall) may not begin commercial operation after July 1, 2025 unless the owner applies to the FAA for aircraft-detection or other light-mitigating technology, and must install it within 24 months of approval; existing systems must apply from January 1, 2026 and install within 60 months of approval.
statute_citation: Idaho Code 21-515B (2025 Idaho Sess. Laws ch. 153, H 146)
amendments_note: Added 2025, ch. 153, sec. 1 (H 146, emergency clause, effective 2025-03-24); no later amendment shown on legislature.idaho.gov as of 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Read 21-515B on legislature.idaho.gov and the enrolled H0146E1.pdf. This is an operating condition rather than a setback; drafted as other. Postdates the June 2024 inventory.
review_note: Read Idaho Code 21-515B (https://legislature.idaho.gov/statutesrules/idstat/Title21/T21CH5/SECT21-515B/), the H0146 bill page and enrolled text H0146E1.pdf on legislature.idaho.gov, 2026-10-09. (1) on and after July 1, 2025 no new wind energy conversion system may commence commercial operations unless the owner applies to the FAA for a light-mitigating technology system, and installs within 24 months of approval; (2) from January 1, 2026 existing systems must apply and install within 60 months of approval; (3) progress notices go to the Idaho Transportation Department division of aeronautics; (5)(b) definition is five or more turbines fifty feet or taller. Section 2 of the bill declares an emergency; bill page shows signed March 24, 2025, Session Law Chapter 153, effective 03/24/2025. History line: added 2025, ch. 153, sec. 1, no later amendment. All fields match. Note: the division of aeronautics only receives progress notices; it does not approve anything, which fits who_decides left blank.

summary: Cities and counties decide siting of wind and solar through planning and zoning. A public utility (electrical corporation) building a plant also needs a certificate from the Idaho Public Utilities Commission, and a local order that conflicts with a specific PUC order is void to the extent of the conflict, but no state body sites merchant wind or solar.
amendments_note: 67-6528 history: added 1975, no later amendment shown; 61-526 history: last am. 1970; both on legislature.idaho.gov as of 2026-10-09. 2025 H 146 (wind lighting) added 21-515B, see ID-other-1. Web searches found no 2025 or 2026 Idaho siting statute for wind or solar (2025 H 317 and H 387 died).
draft_note: Read 67-6528 and 61-526 on legislature.idaho.gov. LBNL calls Idaho "Both"; I drafted local_government because the CPCN in 61-526 binds only regulated electrical corporations and the 67-6528 override applies only where the PUC has issued a specific order. Reviewer may prefer hybrid. 67-6504 not opened.
review_note: Read Idaho Code 67-6528 (https://legislature.idaho.gov/statutesrules/idstat/Title67/T67CH65/SECT67-6528/) and 61-526 (https://legislature.idaho.gov/statutesrules/idstat/Title61/T61CH5/SECT61-526/), 2026-10-09. 61-526: an electrical corporation may not begin construction of a line, plant or system without a PUC certificate of convenience and necessity (with extension exceptions). 67-6528: an action or order of a local agency under titles 31, 50 or 67 that conflicts with a specific PUC order to a public utility is null and void insofar as it conflicts, if the PUC first gave the local agency a chance to appear. Summary matches. local_government is supported: neither section gives a state body siting authority over non-utility (merchant) wind or solar; 67-6504 was not opened by me either. History: 67-6528 added 1975 with no later amendment; 61-526 last am. 1970. Checked the 2026 session subject index on legislature.idaho.gov: wind and solar entries are tax distribution, portable solar devices and solar geoengineering, none a siting statute.

summary: Counties may adopt standards for commercial wind and solar facilities but none more restrictive than the statute, may not ban them (even temporarily) in agricultural or industrial districts, must approve compliant applications, and may not set stricter sound, height, decommissioning or property-value conditions. The law exempts projects filed before 2023-01-27, an industrial enterprise zone near the I-88/I-39 interchange (Lee-Ogle, added by P.A. 103-81) and an area in Madison County (added by P.A. 104-458).

summary: A developer of a wind, solar or storage facility of 50 MW or more in an unincorporated area may petition the Illinois Commerce Commission when a local government violates the state siting law; the Commission may issue a siting certificate if the local government denied the project, missed the statutory deadline, or never adopted a compliant ordinance, and the certificate authorizes construction.

Sound limits may be no stricter than state Pollution Control Board rules.

summary: Counties and municipalities decide siting of wind and solar through local zoning; there is no state siting permit. State default standards apply only in communities that volunteer to become wind or solar energy ready communities (see IN-state_setback_standard-1 and -2).
amendments_note: Not checked on the official site (see note). News reports say 2025 SEA 425 (energy production zones) excludes wind and solar from its zoning bypass; I did not read SEA 425.
draft_note: Local authority is the default under zoning law; I did not open IC 36-7-4 or IC 8-1-8.5-7 (the CPCN exemption LBNL cites). LBNL also cites IC 36-7-2-8 as a limit on local solar restrictions; a 2014 compiled copy (statecodesfiles.justia.com) shows that section covers solar heating and cooling devices only, so I did not draft a preemption row from it. The official site iga.in.gov is a JavaScript app; curl and WebFetch receive only an empty shell (tried https://iga.in.gov/laws/2025/ic/titles/8 and /titles/36 on 2026-10-09), so I could not read the current code or history notes there.
review_note: The draft was snippet-level; I read the official Indiana Code 2026 chapter PDFs on iga.in.gov (the site is a JavaScript app, but its own download links work with browser headers): https://iga.in.gov/ic/2026/Title_8/Article_1/Chapter_8.5.pdf, .../Chapter_8.2.pdf, .../Chapter_41.pdf, .../Chapter_42.pdf and https://iga.in.gov/ic/2026/Title_36/Article_7/Chapter_4.pdf, 2026-10-09. IC 8-1-8.5-2 requires an IURC certificate only for a public utility building generation for public utility service, and 8-1-8.5-7 exempts listed generators (history ends P.L.57-2024); no section gives a state body siting authority over wind or solar. IC 8-1-41-1(d) and 8-1-42-1(d): state default standards apply only in units that voluntarily adopt them. SEA 425-2025 (P.L.202-2025): IC 8-1-8.2-1(b) and 8-1-8.2-2(b) exclude wind power devices and commercial solar energy systems from the energy production zone zoning bypass, as the amendments_note reports. Not in the row and material after June 2024: P.L.202-2025, SEC.21 added IC 36-7-4-1109.5, which from July 1, 2025 limits a local prohibition on generation projects by entities other than retail utilities, their affiliates, REMCs and joint agencies (so merchant wind and solar) to one year, with no extension or renewal. summary: In a county or municipality that voluntarily adopts the state wind standards, turbines must be set back 3 times tip height from nonparticipating homes, 1.1 times from nonparticipating property lines, roads and airport runways, 1 mile from state parks and municipal boundaries (waivable by the municipality), and meet a 50 dBA hourly sound limit at homes; local height limits may be no stricter than FAA rules.
amendments_note: Could not check for amendments after the 2022 printing on iga.in.gov (see note). Web searches found no 2025 or 2026 act amending IC 8-1-41.
draft_note: Read a copy of IC 8-1-41 (pages marked "Indiana Code 2022") posted by the Indiana Office of Energy Development, not the legislature site. Applies only where a unit has opted in under 8-1-41-1. LBNL cites 8-1-41-4 for the default standards, but in this text section 4 defines "permit authority"; the standards are sections 10 to 16. The official site iga.in.gov is a JavaScript app; curl and WebFetch receive only an empty shell (tried https://iga.in.gov/laws/2025/ic/titles/8 and /titles/36 on 2026-10-09), so I could not read the current code or history notes there.
review_note: Read IC 8-1-41 in the official Indiana Code 2026 PDF (https://iga.in.gov/ic/2026/Title_8/Article_1/Chapter_41.pdf) and the 2025 edition, 2026-10-09; also the OED copy at the row's URL. 8-1-41-1(a),(d): sections 10 to 16 (or less restrictive standards) apply only in a unit that voluntarily adopted them (wind energy ready community). 8-1-41-10: (b) 3 times blade tip height from a dwelling on nonparticipating property; (a) 1.1 times from nonparticipating property lines and the centerline of airport runways, public roads and railroads; (e) 1 mile from a state park; (f) 1 mile from municipal corporate boundaries, waivable or reducible by the municipality; (g) tip height limit no stricter than FAA 14 CFR Part 77. 8-1-41-13: 50 dBA hourly average modeled at an affected dwelling. All match. Amendments: every section in the 2026 chapter shows only 'As added by P.L.90-2022, SEC.1'; no change after June 2024. The 2026 code text matches the 2022 OED copy the drafter read.

summary: In a county or municipality that voluntarily adopts the state solar standards, commercial solar must be set back 250 feet from nonparticipating homes (or less with a landscape buffer), 50 feet from nonparticipating property lines and 10 to 40 feet from roads, panels may be no taller than 25 feet at full tilt, and sound may not exceed a 50 dBA hourly average at neighboring homes.
amendments_note: Could not check for amendments after the 2022 printing on iga.in.gov (see note). Web searches found no 2025 or 2026 act amending IC 8-1-42.
draft_note: Read a copy of IC 8-1-42 (pages marked "Indiana Code 2022") posted by the Indiana Office of Energy Development. Applies only where a unit has opted in under 8-1-42-1(d). LBNL cites 8-1-42-6 for the default standards, but section 6 defines "permit authority"; the standards are sections 10 to 20. The official site iga.in.gov is a JavaScript app; curl and WebFetch receive only an empty shell (tried https://iga.in.gov/laws/2025/ic/titles/8 and /titles/36 on 2026-10-09), so I could not read the current code or history notes there.
review_note: Read IC 8-1-42 in the official Indiana Code 2026 PDF (https://iga.in.gov/ic/2026/Title_8/Article_1/Chapter_42.pdf) and the 2025 edition, 2026-10-09; also the OED copy at the row's URL. 8-1-42-1(a),(d): applies only in a unit that voluntarily adopted sections 10 to 20 or less restrictive standards. 8-1-42-10: (b) 250 feet from a dwelling on nonparticipating property; (c) a landscape buffer is required if panels are within 250 feet; (a) 50 feet from nonparticipating property lines, 40 feet from interstate, federal, state or county highway rights-of-way, 30 feet from collector roads and 10 feet from local roads; (d) panels no more than 25 feet at full tilt; (e) setbacks and buffer waivable by the nonparticipating owner. 8-1-42-16: 50 dBA hourly average modeled at a dwelling on adjacent nonparticipating property. All match. Amendments: every section shows only 'As added by P.L.90-2022, SEC.2'; no change after June 2024.

summary: For eminent domain purposes, siting wind turbines or solar generating equipment is not a public utility activity, so neither utilities nor developers may condemn land for these facilities.
amendments_note: Solar was added by L. 2024, ch. 69 (2024 SB 455, conference report carrying SB 457, approved 2024-04-22, eff. July 1); the wind clause predates it (the revisor memo on SB 457 calls it existing law). History line on ksrevisor.gov, 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Read 66-104(g) on ksrevisor.gov. Which 2021 act added the wind clause is from the history line only, not read. Enactment details for 2024 from search results (Kansas Legislature summary pages).
review_note: Read K.S.A. 66-104(g) on ksrevisor.gov (https://www.ksrevisor.gov/statutes/chapters/ch66/066_001_0004.html) and the enrolled 2024 SB 455 (https://www.kslegislature.gov/li_2024/b2023_24/measures/documents/sb455_enrolled.pdf), 2026-10-09. (g): for purposes of the authority to appropriate property through eminent domain, 'public utility' does not include any activity for the siting or placement of (1) wind generators or turbines including towers or (2) solar generation equipment including panels. SB 455's title says it prohibits utilities from exercising eminent domain for solar facilities, and the history line shows L. 2021, ch. 39 and ch. 113 before L. 2024, ch. 69, consistent with wind predating solar. No 2025 or 2026 amendment (revisor composite lists). Wording note for the drafter: the statute only removes public-utility status for this purpose; 'neither utilities nor developers may condemn land' is the practical effect rather than the statute's words, and the approval date 2024-04-22 is not shown in the documents I read.

summary: Cities and counties decide siting of wind and solar through planning and zoning; a merchant generator built after 2001 that is not in a regulated rate base may opt out of Kansas Corporation Commission jurisdiction, so no state body sites these projects.
amendments_note: 12-741 history: L. 1991 only. 66-104 history ends L. 2024, ch. 69 (solar eminent domain, see KS-other-1). As shown on ksrevisor.gov 2026-10-09. 2025 SB 233 (county decommissioning agreements) appears to have stalled in committee (search result only).
draft_note: Read 12-741 and 66-104 on ksrevisor.gov. Roughly half of Kansas counties are unzoned (developer testimony, not verified).
review_note: Read K.S.A. 12-741 (https://www.ksrevisor.gov/statutes/chapters/ch12/012_007_0041.html) and 66-104 (https://www.ksrevisor.gov/statutes/chapters/ch66/066_001_0004.html) on ksrevisor.gov, 2026-10-09. 12-741(a): enabling act for city and county planning and zoning. 66-104(e)(1): at the entity's option, 'public utility' excludes generation, marketing and sale from a facility newly placed in service on or after January 1, 2001 that is not in the rate base of a rate-regulated utility, cooperative or municipal utility. To test 'no state body sites these projects' I read the only Kansas generation siting act, K.S.A. 66-1,158 and 66-1,159: it covers nuclear generation facilities only. History: 12-741 L. 1991 only; 66-104 ends L. 2024, ch. 69. The revisor's 2026 and 2025 composite lists of new, amended and repealed statutes show no change to 12-741 or 66-104 and no wind or solar siting statute (2026 entries in chapter 12 are the by-right housing act, SB 418; 66-104h, SB 348, exempts certain cooperative subsidiaries).

state_body: Kentucky State Board on Electric Generation and Transmission Siting
summary: Since 2026-07-15 an applicant for a wind facility certificate must certify that turbines will not be artificially lit except as required by law and that shadow flicker will be minimized and will not significantly harm neighboring uses, and the board considers compliance when deciding.
amendments_note: Added by 2026 Ky. Acts ch. 152, ss26-27 (HB 677, eff. 2026-07-15); 278.706 also amended by ch. 198, s57. Postdates the inventory.
draft_note: Read KRS 278.706 and 278.710 history notes and the lighting/flicker text on apps.legislature.ky.gov.
review_note: Read KRS 278.706 (https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=57883) and 278.710 (id=57884), both effective July 15, 2026, plus 2026 Ky. Acts ch. 152 and 2023 Ky. Acts ch. 140 on apps.legislature.ky.gov, 2026-10-09. 278.706(2)(n): a wind facility application must certify that turbines will not be artificially lighted except as required by law, that facilities are sited to minimize shadowing or flicker, and that any shadowing or flicker will not have a significant adverse impact on neighboring uses; 278.710(1)(k): the board decides based in part on whether the applicant will comply with those certifications. The 2023 act's version of 278.706(2) ends at (m), and the (n) text appears in 2026 Act 152, so 'since 2026-07-15' is supported. History: 278.706 am. 2026 ch. 152, s26 and ch. 198, s57; 278.710 am. 2026 ch. 152, s27. Board name and wind:10 threshold (278.700(2)) match.

state_body: Kentucky State Board on Electric Generation and Transmission Siting
summary: A merchant generating facility of 10 MW or more that sells at wholesale needs a construction certificate from the state siting board, and local ordinances, permits and planning and zoning setbacks still apply and prevail over a conflicting board order. Smaller facilities are left to local government.
amendments_note: 278.704 and 278.718 amended by 2026 Ky. Acts ch. 152 (HB 677, became law without signature 2026-04-14, eff. 2026-07-15), and 278.704 also by ch. 198 (HB 869). 278.700 last amended 2014. Per KRS history notes on apps.legislature.ky.gov, 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Read KRS 278.700, 278.704, 278.718 on apps.legislature.ky.gov. LBNL says the board "cannot modify or waive local setback requirements"; KRS 278.718 goes further, giving local ordinances primacy over board orders. The 10 MW threshold applies only to merchant (non-PSC-regulated) facilities.
review_note: Read KRS 278.700 (https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=42952), 278.704 (id=57882), 278.718 (id=57886) and the HB 677 record (https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/record/26rs/hb677.html), 2026-10-09. 278.700(1) names the Kentucky State Board on Electric Generation and Transmission Siting; 278.700(2) merchant facility is 10 MW or more aggregate selling at wholesale at rates not regulated by the PSC; 278.704(1) no construction without a board certificate; 278.704(3) local planning and zoning may set height, decommissioning and setbacks with primacy; 278.718 local ordinances, permits and licenses have primacy over 278.700 to 278.708 and conflicts are resolved for the local government. All fields match. Amendments: 278.704 and 278.718 show 2026 Ky. Acts ch. 152 (secs. 25, 29) and 278.704 also ch. 198, sec. 56, effective July 15, 2026; 278.700 last amended 2014; the HB 677 record says 'became law without Governor's Signature (Acts Ch. 152)' on 04/14/26. The text read is the post-2026 text.

state_body: Kentucky State Board on Electric Generation and Transmission Siting
summary: A siting board certificate may not issue unless any wind turbine is at least 1,000 feet from adjoining property lines and all generating structures are 2,000 feet from any residential neighborhood, school, hospital or nursing home; since 2026-07-15 wind turbine hub height is capped at 350 feet. Local planning and zoning limits take precedence where adopted, and the board may grant deviations from the state distances.
amendments_note: Amended by 2026 Ky. Acts ch. 152, s25 (HB 677, eff. 2026-07-15): added the 350-foot hub height limit and decommissioning bond carve-out; also 2026 ch. 198, s56 (HB 869), codified together. Earlier: 2023 Ky. Acts ch. 140 and 2014 Ky. Acts ch. 88 (HB 291, the source Sabin cites).
draft_note: Read KRS 278.704 on apps.legislature.ky.gov and Act 152 (2026) section 25. Act 152 inserted "or storage" in the 2,000-foot clause, but the codified text I read says only "generation"; ch. 198 may have changed it. Reviewer should check. Applies to facilities subject to the board (10 MW merchant).
review_note: Read KRS 278.704 (https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=57882, effective July 15, 2026), 2026 Ky. Acts ch. 152 (https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/acts/26RS/documents/0152.pdf) section 25, and 2023 Ky. Acts ch. 140 (.../23RS/documents/0140.pdf) section 2, 2026-10-09. 278.704(2)(a): no certificate unless the exhaust stack and any wind turbine are at least 1,000 feet from an adjoining property boundary, all structures used for generation are 2,000 feet from any residential neighborhood, school, hospital or nursing home, and wind hub height does not exceed 350 feet; (3) local planning and zoning height, decommissioning and setback limits have primacy and cannot be waived by the board; (4) the board may grant deviations from subsection (2). The 2023 act has no hub-height limit, so the 350-foot cap is new in 2026 as the row says. On the drafter's question: Act 152 inserted 'or storage' in (2)(a)2, but the codified text (Act 152 and HB 869, ch. 198, codified together per the LRC note) reads 'generation of electricity' only, which matches the summary. Thresholds 10 MW follow from 278.700(2).

state_body: Louisiana Department of Conservation and Energy
summary: Parish and municipal zoning governs siting, and the state Department of Conservation and Energy must also permit solar facilities of 10 acres or more (decommissioning and bonding), solar facilities of 75 acres or more (siting standards), every onshore wind project and renewable energy batteries (rules due by 2026-08-31).
amendments_note: 30:1131, 30:1141 to 30:1145 enacted by 2025 La. Acts No. 279 (HB 459, eff. 2025-08-01). 30:1154 last amended by 2023 Acts No. 150 and No. 455. The department was renamed from Energy and Natural Resources to Conservation and Energy. No 2026 act shown in the history notes on legis.la.gov as of 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Read 30:1131, 30:1141, 30:1142, 30:1143 and 30:1154 on legis.la.gov and Act 279 (ViewDocument.aspx?d=1425593). Thresholds are acres, not MW, so threshold_mw is blank. The 30:1154 permit covers only the decommissioning plan and financial security.
review_note: Read La. R.S. 30:1131 (https://legis.la.gov/Legis/Law.aspx?d=1432740), 30:1141 (d=1432741), 30:1142 (d=1432742), 30:1143 (d=1432743, the row's URL), 30:1144 (d=1432747), 30:1145 (d=1432748) and 30:1154 (d=86925) on legis.la.gov, 2026-10-09. 30:1154(D)(1): solar of 10 or more acres needs a department permit that pertains only to the decommissioning plan and financial security; 30:1143(A): solar of 75 or more acres needs a permit under the new Part; 30:1141(A): no onshore wind project without a Department of Conservation and Energy permit (residential excluded); 30:1131(A),(C): renewable energy batteries need a permit, rules due by August 31, 2026 (residential excluded); 30:1142(B): a parish with solar ordinances may opt out of the siting standards, consistent with local zoning continuing to apply. Department name, acreage thresholds (threshold_mw rightly blank) and hybrid match. History: 30:1131 and 30:1141 to 30:1145 show only Acts 2025, No. 279, s1; 30:1154 ends Acts 2023, No. 150 and No. 455. No 2026 act shown.

state_body: Louisiana Department of Conservation and Energy
summary: Solar facilities of 75 acres or more outside industrial-zoned or certified sites, begun after 2026-01-01, must keep 300 feet from residential property lines (with a 35 to 50 foot vegetative barrier) unless the owner agrees otherwise, 100 feet from water bodies and 50 feet from roads, and may not raise noise more than 10 dBA above ambient at the property line. A parish with its own solar ordinance may opt out of these standards by resolution.
amendments_note: Enacted by 2025 La. Acts No. 279 (HB 459, eff. 2025-08-01); no later amendment shown on legis.la.gov as of 2026-10-09. Postdates the inventory.
draft_note: Read 30:1142 and 30:1144 on legis.la.gov. The parish opt-out lets a parish replace the state standards with its own ordinance; it is not a bar on facilities, so I did not draft a local_opt_out row.
review_note: Read La. R.S. 30:1144 (https://legis.la.gov/Legis/Law.aspx?d=1432747) and 30:1142 (d=1432742) on legis.la.gov, 2026-10-09. 30:1144(A): solar of 75 acres or more not wholly within an industrial-zoned area or a Louisiana Economic Development certified site; (B)(2) 300 feet from residential property lines unless a written agreement provides otherwise, with a 35-foot barrier of new plants or a 50-foot barrier of natural plants; (B)(3) 100 feet from the ordinary low water mark of natural and navigable water bodies; (B)(4) 50 feet from the edge of paved public roads with a 35-foot barrier; (C) noise at the property line no more than 10 dBA above pre-operation ambient; (D) applies where construction begins after January 1, 2026. 30:1142(B): a parish that has adopted solar ordinances may opt out by resolution. All values match. History: Acts 2025, No. 279, s1 only; no later amendment shown.

summary: No local zoning ordinance or bylaw may prohibit or unreasonably regulate solar energy systems except where necessary to protect public health, safety or welfare.
amendments_note: St. 2024, c. 239 section 37 replaced "department of public utilities" with "energy facilities siting board" in the public service corporation zoning exemption paragraphs of section 3; the solar sentence itself is unchanged in the text shown on malegislature.gov as of 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Read ch. 40A section 3 on malegislature.gov (solar paragraph). Ch. 25A section 21(b) refers to "limitations on solar facility and small clean energy storage facility zoning under section 3 of chapter 40A", but the section 3 text I read contains no storage language; reviewer may want to check whether a storage clause was added elsewhere. The same section also lets the EFSB exempt public service corporation facilities from local zoning (not separately drafted).
review_note: Read M.G.L. c.40A s.3 at https://malegislature.gov/Laws/GeneralLaws/PartI/TitleVII/Chapter40A/Section3 on 2026-10-09: No zoning ordinance or by-law shall prohibit or unreasonably regulate the installation of solar energy systems or the building of structures that facilitate the collection of solar energy, except where necessary to protect the public health, safety or welfare. Summary, technology (solar) and citation match. Amendment note checked in St. 2024 c.239 s.37 (strikes department of public utilities and inserts energy facilities siting board in the public service corporation exemption paragraphs); the current text shows energy facilities siting board there and the solar sentence is unchanged. The current s.3 text contains no storage clause, despite the cross-reference in c.25A s.21(b); no other amendment shown as of 2026-10-09.

summary: For large clean energy facilities, the siting board consolidated permit stands in for all municipal, regional and state permits, and is deemed granted if the board misses its deadline; for small facilities, local governments must apply uniform state standards and a missed 12-month deadline produces a constructive approval.
statute_citation: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 164, sections 69G and 69T(i); ch. 25A, section 21(b), (d) to (g)
amendments_note: New law after the inventory: St. 2024, c. 239 section 74 (69T, effective March 1, 2026) and section 23 (25A section 21). None later shown on malegislature.gov as of 2026-10-09.
draft_note: 69G defines "consolidated permit" as one that includes all municipal, regional and state permits the facility would otherwise need; 69T(i) caps board review at 15 months and requires a permit with standard conditions if no decision issues. 25A section 21(e)-(g) routes appeals and under-resourced towns to de novo adjudication by the EFSB siting division director under 69W.
review_note: Read on malegislature.gov 2026-10-09: c.164 s.69G definition of Consolidated permit (includes all municipal, regional and state permits the facility would otherwise need, except certain federal permits delegated to state agencies), s.69T(a) and (i) (15-month cap; if no final decision issues the board shall issue a permit granting approval to construct with the common conditions; permit is a composite of all individual permits), and c.25A s.21(b) (uniform standards local governments shall require), (d)(2) (constructive approval permit after 12 months), (e) to (g) (de novo review by the siting division director). Summary, who_decides state_board for the large-facility route, state_body, threshold_mw solar:25;wind:25, technology and citations match. Minor: the summary's all municipal, regional and state permits omits the statutory exception for certain delegated federal permits. Enactment by St. 2024 c.239 s.23 and s.74, effective March 1, 2026 (s.139), confirmed in the session law; no later amendment shown as of 2026-10-09.

summary: The Energy Facilities Siting Board issues a single consolidated permit for solar and wind facilities of 25 MW or more (solar measured in DC) and storage of 100 MWh or more; smaller clean energy facilities are permitted by the city or town under uniform state standards, with a 12-month deadline and de novo review by the siting division director.
statute_citation: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 164, sections 69G and 69T; ch. 25A, section 21 (as added or amended by St. 2024, c. 239)
amendments_note: Changed after the inventory: St. 2024, c. 239 (signed Nov. 2024) section 74 added ch. 164 sections 69T to 69W, effective March 1, 2026 (c. 239 section 139), and section 23 added ch. 25A section 21. Section 132 says EFSB regulations apply to projects submitted on and after July 1, 2026. Section 69G now defines "generating facility" and "large clean energy generation facility" at 25 MW, replacing the 100 MW threshold the inventory describes. No later amendment shown in the section notes on malegislature.gov as of 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Read on malegislature.gov: ch. 164 section 69G (definitions: large clean energy generation facility 25 MW or more; large clean energy storage facility 100 MWh or more), section 69T (consolidated permits), sections 69U and 69W; ch. 25A section 21 (small facilities under 25 MW / under 100 MWh, local consolidated permit, 12 months, constructive approval); and session law St. 2024 c. 239 sections 23, 74, 118, 132, 139. The inventory says 100 MW; that was the pre-2024 law. Storage threshold is in MWh (100 MWh), so it is not in threshold_mw. The local consolidated permit under 25A section 21(c) is elective for the applicant. I did not identify which c. 239 section rewrote the 69G thresholds; the section page shows the current text only.
review_note: Read on malegislature.gov 2026-10-09: M.G.L. c.164 s.69G (Generating facility 25 MW or more; Large clean energy generation facility nameplate not less than 25 MW, solar, wind or anaerobic digestion, solar capacity in direct current; Large clean energy storage facility not less than 100 MWh), s.69T (https://malegislature.gov/Laws/GeneralLaws/PartI/TitleXXII/Chapter164/Section69T: no construction of a large clean energy infrastructure facility without a board consolidated permit; 15-month cap), c.25A s.21 (small facilities under 25 MW and under 100 MWh; uniform standards local governments shall require; 12-month local decision; de novo adjudication by the siting division director under 69W), and session law St. 2024 c.239 (https://malegislature.gov/Laws/SessionLaws/Acts/2024/Chapter239, approved Nov. 20, 2024). Confirmed in c.239: s.23 adds 25A s.21; s.56 changes the 69G generating facility figure from 100 to 25; s.57 adds the large clean energy definitions; s.74 adds 69T to 69W; s.132 regulations apply to projects submitted on and after July 1, 2026; s.139 effective March 1, 2026 (69T page header says the same). who_decides hybrid, state_body, threshold_mw solar:25;wind:25, technology and citation all match. Note: the local consolidated application under 25A s.21(c) is elective, so the 12-month deadline applies to that route. No later amendment shown on the official pages as of 2026-10-09.

summary: Local governments may not adopt zoning that prohibits solar generating stations (over 1 MW, wholesale or community solar) or deny site plans that meet the state siting standards, must expedite review, and must treat projects of 5 MW or less as a permitted use, subject to the growth-area and priority preservation exceptions in MD-other-1.
amendments_note: Enacted by 2025 Md. Laws ch. 623 (SB 931, Renewable Energy Certainty Act, eff. 2025-07-01; HB 1036 is ch. 624). 2026 bills to change it (HB 460 lowering the priority preservation cap to 2 percent, SB 683, SB 265) show no action after committee hearings on mgaleg.maryland.gov as of 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Read PUA 7-218 on mgaleg.maryland.gov. Sabin REC-0171 describes the 2019 Court of Appeals holding that state law preempts local zoning for PSC-certified solar; RECA now states the preemption in statute.
review_note: Read Md. Code, Pub. Util. 7-218 on mgaleg.maryland.gov (https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/mgawebsite/Laws/StatuteText?article=gpu&section=7-218) and 7-207(h), 2026-10-09. 7-218(b): applies to solar over 1 MW AC selling wholesale, community solar or aggregate net metering, not on rooftops, carports, brownfields or behind the meter. (h)(1): except as in (h)(3) and (4), a local jurisdiction may not adopt zoning that prohibits construction or operation of these stations or deny site plans meeting subsection (f); (h)(2): it must expedite review and process stations of not more than 5 MW as a permitted use. Summary matches (its 'wholesale or community solar' omits aggregate net metering, which is also covered; not an error). Amendments: enacted by 2025 ch. 623 (SB 931) and ch. 624 (HB 1036), effective July 1, 2025; 2026 bills HB 460, SB 683 and SB 265 show hearings only and no chapter.

summary: Local governments may not adopt zoning that prohibits front-of-the-meter energy storage or deny site plans that meet the state requirements, and must expedite review and adopt standard review processes.
amendments_note: Enacted by 2025 Md. Laws ch. 623 (SB 931, Renewable Energy Certainty Act, eff. 2025-07-01; HB 1036 is ch. 624). 2026 bills to change it (HB 460 lowering the priority preservation cap to 2 percent, SB 683, SB 265) show no action after committee hearings on mgaleg.maryland.gov as of 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Read PUA 7-219 on mgaleg.maryland.gov. Postdates the inventory.
review_note: Read Md. Code, Pub. Util. 7-219 on mgaleg.maryland.gov (https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/mgawebsite/Laws/StatuteText?article=gpu&section=7-219), 2026-10-09. 7-219(f)(1): a local jurisdiction may not adopt zoning or other laws that prohibit construction or operation of front-of-the-meter energy storage devices, or deny site plans that meet subsection (e); (f)(2): it shall expedite review of compliant plans and adopt standard review processes. Summary, technology and local_government match. Amendments: added by the Renewable Energy Certainty Act, 2025 ch. 623 (SB 931) and ch. 624 (HB 1036), effective July 1, 2025 per the bill pages; no 2026 chapter found for the 2026 solar bills.

summary: Ground-mounted solar over 5 MW may not be sited on land that on 2025-01-01 was in a Tier 1 or Tier 2 growth area, a medium or high density residential area, or a mixed-use area with homes, and solar in a priority preservation area established before 2025 is capped at 5 percent of that area's acreage.
amendments_note: Enacted by 2025 Md. Laws ch. 623 (SB 931, Renewable Energy Certainty Act, eff. 2025-07-01; HB 1036 is ch. 624). 2026 bills to change it (HB 460 lowering the priority preservation cap to 2 percent, SB 683, SB 265) show no action after committee hearings on mgaleg.maryland.gov as of 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Read PUA 7-218(h)(3)-(4) on mgaleg.maryland.gov. The 5 MW figure applies to the growth and residential area bar; the 5 percent cap applies to all covered solar.
review_note: Read Md. Code, Pub. Util. 7-218(h)(3),(4) on mgaleg.maryland.gov (https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/mgawebsite/Laws/StatuteText?article=gpu&section=7-218), 2026-10-09. (h)(3): ground-mounted solar over 5 MW AC may not be located on land that on January 1, 2025 was in a Tier 1 or Tier 2 growth area, a medium or high density residential area, or a mixed-use area with a residential component; (h)(4): stations approved in a priority preservation area established before January 1, 2025 are limited to 5 percent of its acreage. Summary matches. Note for the drafter, not a field error: scripts/state_policies.py defines threshold_mw as a size that splits state and local authority; here 5 MW is the scope of a siting bar rather than an authority split, and the 5 percent cap applies to all solar covered by 7-218(b), as the draft_note says. Amendments: 2025 ch. 623 (SB 931) and ch. 624 (HB 1036), effective July 1, 2025; HB 460 (2026), which would lower the cap, shows a hearing only and no chapter.

summary: Grid-connected generating stations need a certificate of public convenience and necessity (or an exemption or distributed generation certificate) from the Public Service Commission, and front-of-meter storage needs Commission approval; for wholesale or community solar of 1 to 2 MW the local jurisdiction checks the state siting standards instead. Counties still issue local permits but may not require conditional use or special exception approval.
amendments_note: Enacted by 2025 Md. Laws ch. 623 (SB 931, Renewable Energy Certainty Act, eff. 2025-07-01; HB 1036 is ch. 624). 2026 bills to change it (HB 460 lowering the priority preservation cap to 2 percent, SB 683, SB 265) show no action after committee hearings on mgaleg.maryland.gov as of 2026-10-09. 7-207 also carries a contingency note for 2025 ch. 572 (two versions shown).
draft_note: Read PUA 7-207 (version marked in effect), 7-218 and 7-219 on mgaleg.maryland.gov. Drafted hybrid because solar of 2 MW or less is verified locally and larger solar goes to the PSC; wind and storage go to the PSC with no MW floor (7-207 excludes only small off-grid units). LBNL says State.
review_note: Read Md. Code, Pub. Util. 7-207 (version marked CONTINGENCY IN EFFECT, ch. 572 of 2025), 7-218 and 7-219 on mgaleg.maryland.gov (https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/mgawebsite/Laws/StatuteText?article=gpu&section=7-207, ...7-218, ...7-219), and the SB 931 and HB 1036 (2025) bill pages, 2026-10-09. 7-207(b)(1): no construction of a generating station without a PSC CPCN, unless the person obtains 7-207.1 approval or a 7-207.4 distributed generation CPCN; 7-207(a)(4) excludes only small units that cannot export during outages and some behind-the-meter combinations, so wind has no MW floor. 7-218(b),(c): for solar over 1 MW selling wholesale, community solar or aggregate net metering, the Commission verifies the site requirements, or the local jurisdiction does for stations of not more than 2 MW, and a CPCN, DG CPCN or 7-207.1 approval is required above 2 MW, so solar:2 correctly marks the state and local split. 7-219(b): front-of-the-meter storage needs Commission approval. 7-207(h)(1),(3): counties approve local permits but may not require conditional use, special exception or floating zone approval. Amendments: SB 931 is Chapter 623 and HB 1036 Chapter 624 (Renewable Energy Certainty Act), effective July 1, 2025. The 2026 bills HB 460, SB 683 and SB 265 show only hearings (2/10, 2/26, 2/19) and no chapter number.

summary: Solar generating stations over 1 MW (other than agrivoltaics) must keep 150 feet from homes and 100 feet from property lines, keep fencing at most 20 feet tall and 50 feet from roads, provide a vegetative buffer up to 35 feet wide, emit no visible light at night, and average no more than 15 feet in height; a county siting agreement may set looser terms.
amendments_note: Enacted by 2025 Md. Laws ch. 623 (SB 931, Renewable Energy Certainty Act, eff. 2025-07-01; HB 1036 is ch. 624). 2026 bills to change it (HB 460 lowering the priority preservation cap to 2 percent, SB 683, SB 265) show no action after committee hearings on mgaleg.maryland.gov as of 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Read PUA 7-218(f) on mgaleg.maryland.gov. Postdates the inventory.
review_note: Read Md. Code, Pub. Util. 7-218(b),(f) on mgaleg.maryland.gov (https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/mgawebsite/Laws/StatuteText?article=gpu&section=7-218), 2026-10-09. (f)(1) excludes agrivoltaics; (f)(2)(i) 150 feet to the nearest wall of a residential dwelling; (ii) 100 feet to property lines (not internal lines of the project area); (iii) nonbarbed fencing not more than 20 feet high and not less than 50 feet from a public road right-of-way; (iv),(4)(i) landscape buffer not more than 35 feet wide; (7) no visible light dusk to dawn except as required for law, safety or emergency; (8) average height not more than 15 feet (not applied to stations on land also used for agriculture); (10) a county siting agreement with less stringent terms satisfies the subsection. All values match; scope is solar over 1 MW under (b). Amendments: 2025 ch. 623 and ch. 624, effective July 1, 2025; no 2026 chapter found.

summary: A solar development approved under the Site Location of Development Act on high-value agricultural land must pay a compensation fee based on the affected area (reducible for dual-use agrivoltaics) or permanently conserve an equal area of farmland.
amendments_note: Enacted by PL 2023, c. 448; amended by PL 2025, c. 597, Pt. A, s59 (agency renaming). As shown on legislature.maine.gov 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Read 38 M.R.S. 484-C on legislature.maine.gov. Not in the inventory.
review_note: Read 38 M.R.S. 484-C on legislature.maine.gov (https://legislature.maine.gov/statutes/38/title38sec484-C.html), 2026-10-09. 484-C(1): a person who obtains approval under the Site Location of Development article for a solar energy development on high-value agricultural land must pay a compensation fee or other compensation for the impacted area; (2) fee based on square footage and fair market value, reducible for mitigation including dual-use agricultural and solar production (and increasable for severe impacts); (4) the applicant may instead conserve an equal area by perpetual easement or fee ownership that keeps it available for agriculture. Summary, technology, DEP and policy type match. History: PL 2023, c. 448, s1 (NEW); PL 2025, c. 597, Pt. A, s59 (AMD), which changed the agency named in (2) to the Department of Energy Resources; no change to the requirement.

summary: The Department of Environmental Protection permits wind and solar developments that meet the Site Location of Development Act size triggers (more than 20 acres, or buildings, roads, paved areas and stripped or graded areas not revegetated covering more than 3 acres), and is the primary siting authority for grid-scale wind under the Wind Energy Act, while municipalities also regulate through their own ordinances.
amendments_note: 38 M.R.S. 482 section history ends PL 2023, c. 481, ss12-14 (offshore wind terminal) and PL 2025, c. 554, s1 (amends the subdivision definition, not the acreage triggers in 482(2)(A), (C) or 482(6)(B)). 35-A M.R.S. 3451 history ends PL 2023, c. 481, s9 and PL 2023, c. 369, Pt. A, ss4-5, with no 2025 entry. 35-A M.R.S. 3454 shows PL 2025, c. 597, Pt. A, ss44-45. 38 M.R.S. 488 shows 2025 amendments (PL 2025, c. 262, c. 388, c. 412, c. 554) on housing, growth-area and Midcoast exemptions, none on wind or solar. As shown on legislature.maine.gov (data extracted 2026-10-05), read 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Corrects the 2026-10-09 draft after review: amendments_note now matches the section histories, which I re-read (482 ends PL 2025, c. 554, s1, not PL 2023, c. 481; 3451 has no 2025 entry; only 3454 shows PL 2025, c. 597); the summary now gives the full 482(6)(B) structure definition instead of 'impervious structures'; statute_citation narrowed to the subsections relied on. I agree with the reviewer. Read 2026-10-09 on legislature.maine.gov: 38 M.R.S. 482 (title38sec482.html), 488 (title38sec488.html), 35-A M.R.S. 3451 and 3454. 482(2)(J) separately covers offshore wind of 3 MW or more in coastal wetlands; threshold_mw is left blank because the land-based triggers are acreage, not MW. 3451(8)(B) makes the Land Use Planning Commission, not the department, the siting authority for wind in unorganized areas that is not grid-scale. 488(19) lets some 3 to 10 acre structures in municipalities with review capacity be reviewed locally instead. The local half of hybrid rests on nothing in these sections displacing municipal ordinances; I did not read the municipal home rule or zoning statutes (30-A M.R.S. 3001, 4352).
review_note: Read 2026-10-09 on legislature.maine.gov (data extracted 10/05/2026): 38 M.R.S. 482 (title38sec482.html), 483-A, 488, 35-A M.R.S. 3451 and 3454, 30-A M.R.S. 3001. Matches: 482(2)(A) land or water area in excess of 20 acres; 482(2)(C) a structure; 482(6)(B) buildings, parking lots, roads, paved areas, wharves or areas stripped or graded and not revegetated over 3 acres; threshold_mw blank is right (acreage triggers; 482(2)(J) offshore wind of 3 MW or more is separate); municipal ordinance power exists under 30-A M.R.S. 3001 (home rule), supporting the local half of hybrid. Amendments_note checks out: 482 history ends PL 2023 c. 481 ss12-14 and PL 2025 c. 554 s1 (subdivision definition only); 3451 ends PL 2023 c. 481 s9 and PL 2023 c. 369 Pt. A ss4-5; 3454 shows PL 2025 c. 597 Pt. A ss44-45; 488 shows PL 2025 c. 262, c. 388, c. 412, c. 554, none on wind or solar. Disagreements: (1) summary says the department 'is the primary siting authority for grid-scale wind under the Wind Energy Act'; 3451(8)(A) makes the department primary siting authority only 'in the case of an expedited wind energy development', which 3451(4) defines as grid-scale wind energy development (or an offshore wind port facility) 'proposed for location within an expedited permitting area' (3451(3): organized areas plus specified places in unorganized areas). Grid-scale wind outside the expedited permitting area is still reviewed by the department under the Site Law (488(9-A)) but the department is not the defined primary siting authority there. The summary should say expedited (grid-scale, in the expedited permitting area) wind, and the citation should add 3451(3), (4). (2) statute_citation cites only the 482 definitions; the requirement that a development get department approval before construction is 38 M.R.S. 483-A(1) ('A person may not construct ... any development of state or regional significance that may substantially affect the environment without first having obtained approval ... from the department'), which is not cited.

summary: No state agency or municipality may license, permit, lease or grant rights for an offshore wind turbine in state-owned submerged lands or territorial waters, except small short-term research turbines, the designated research array project, and port facilities or cables serving wind projects in federal waters.
amendments_note: Enacted by PL 2021, c. 407 (emergency, signed 2021-07-06); amended by PL 2025, c. 597, Pt. A, s33 (rename of the former Governor's Energy Office; no change to the prohibition). As shown on legislature.maine.gov 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Read 35-A M.R.S. 3405 on legislature.maine.gov and the LD 1619 bill and amendments (getPDF.asp). The enacted law is a permanent prohibition, not the 10-year moratorium of the bill as introduced.
review_note: Read 35-A M.R.S. 3405 on legislature.maine.gov (https://legislature.maine.gov/statutes/35-A/title35-Asec3405.html), 2026-10-09. 3405(2): notwithstanding any law, a state agency or municipality may not license, permit, approve, lease or grant an easement for a windmill or wind turbine or tower for an offshore wind power project in state-owned submerged lands or territorial waters. 3405(3) exempts (A) pilot-scale research projects of no more than 0.5 MW operating no more than 5 years, (B) the offshore wind energy demonstration project in the Maine Offshore Wind Energy Research Center with a commission-approved PPA, (C) portside infrastructure and associated facilities for projects seaward of territorial waters, and (D) cables and transmission lines for such projects, conditioned on three Energy Office tasks done by March 1, 2023. Summary matches; state_moratorium covers 'State moratorium or ban' in scripts/state_policies.py. History: PL 2021, c. 407, s2 (NEW); PL 2025, c. 597, Pt. A, s33 (AMD), which amends 3(D) to say 'former Governor's Energy Office'; no change to the prohibition.

summary: State rule limits sound from routine operation of grid-scale and small-scale wind developments to 55 dBA by day and 42 dBA at night at protected locations, and 75 dBA at the project property line.
amendments_note: Rule amendment dates not shown on the copy read; not checked against the Secretary of State rule text.
draft_note: Read the rule on law.cornell.edu (LII copy, not the official Secretary of State text; maine.gov/sos/cec/rules/06/096/096c375.docx returned HTTP 404 on 2026-10-09). This is a state rule, not a statute.
review_note: Read the official rule from the Secretary of State, 06-096 C.M.R. ch. 375 (https://www.maine.gov/sos/sites/maine.gov.sos/files/inline-files/096c375-2025-163.docx, linked from maine.gov/sos/rulemaking/agency-rules/department-environmental-protection-rules) and the LII copy at the row's URL, 2026-10-09. Section 10(I)(1) applies to grid-scale (35-A s3451(6)) and small-scale (s3456) wind energy developments; 10(I)(2): routine-operation sound may not exceed (a) 75 dBA at any time at the development's property line or contiguous developer-controlled property, whichever is farther, and (b) 55 dBA from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. and 42 dBA from 7 p.m. to 7 a.m. at any protected location. All values match. Amendment found that the draft did not check: the rule history lists 'AMENDED: September 14, 2025, filing 2025-163 (Major Substantive Rule)'; the official text after that amendment still has the same wind limits, so the row stands. The amendments_note should be updated to say this.

summary: When the commission issues a certificate, it preempts any local rule that prohibits, regulates or is more restrictive than the certificate, and zoning changes made after the application cannot limit the facility; local ordinances also may not bar site testing.
amendments_note: Added by 2023 PA 233, effective Nov. 29, 2024. No amendment shown in the section history on legislature.mi.gov as of 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Read MCL 460.1231(1)-(5). The inventory cites the preemption as "section 232" of PA 233; in the compiled code it is MCL 460.1231 (section 231), while 460.1232 only applies MCL 8.5 (severability).
review_note: Read MCL 460.1231(1) to (5) at https://www.legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=mcl-460-1231 on 2026-10-09. (1) a local ordinance shall not prohibit or regulate testing activities; (2) a zoning ordinance or limitation imposed after the certificate application shall not limit the facility; (3) the certificate and the part preempt a local policy or ordinance that prohibits, regulates, or imposes additional or more restrictive requirements than those in the certificate. Summary, who_decides, state_body, thresholds (from 460.1222) and citation match. History: Add. 2023, Act 233, Eff. Nov. 29, 2024; no later amendment (MCL complete through PA 103 of 2026).

summary: Developers of solar of 50 MW or more, wind of 100 MW or more, or storage of 50 MW and 200 MWh or more may seek a siting certificate from the Public Service Commission, and a local unit may ask the commission to require one; if the local unit has a compatible renewable energy ordinance the developer must apply locally first, and smaller projects stay under local zoning.
amendments_note: Sections added by 2023 PA 233, effective Nov. 29, 2024 (after the inventory was written, as the inventory notes). No amendment shown in the section history on legislature.mi.gov as of 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Read MCL 460.1221 (definitions, including "compatible renewable energy ordinance": no more restrictive than 460.1226(8); a local moratorium makes the ordinance incompatible), 460.1222 (thresholds; certificate is optional for the developer: "may"), 460.1223 (local route and 120-day deadline; fallback to the commission). City or village exemption in 460.1222(4).
review_note: Read MCL 460.1222 (https://www.legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=mcl-460-1222), 460.1223 and 460.1221 on legislature.mi.gov (MCL complete through PA 103 of 2026) on 2026-10-09. 460.1222(1): solar 50 MW or more, wind 100 MW or more, storage 50 MW or more and 200 MWh or more; (2) developer may obtain a certificate and a local unit exercising zoning may request the commission to require one. 460.1223(3): if the local unit has a compatible renewable energy ordinance the developer shall file with the local unit first (120-day decision, fallback to the commission). Projects below the thresholds are outside the part. who_decides hybrid, state_body, threshold_mw solar:50;wind:100;battery_storage:50, technology and citations match. History on each section: Add. 2023, Act 233, Eff. Nov. 29, 2024; no later amendment.

summary: Certificated facilities must meet statutory standards: solar and storage 300 ft from nonparticipating dwellings and 50 ft from property lines and roads, solar panels no taller than 25 ft, wind turbines 2.1 times tip height from nonparticipating residences, 30 hours a year shadow flicker, and 55 dBA at nonparticipating dwellings. A local ordinance stricter than these standards is not "compatible".
amendments_note: Added by 2023 PA 233, effective Nov. 29, 2024. No amendment shown in the section history on legislature.mi.gov as of 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Read MCL 460.1226(8)(a)-(c). The standards apply as the public health and safety finding for a commission certificate; through the 460.1221(f) definition they also cap what a "compatible" local ordinance may require, but local units without a compatible ordinance keep their own zoning for projects that do not seek a certificate. The inventory does not describe these standards.
review_note: Read MCL 460.1226(8) at https://www.legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=mcl-460-1226 and 460.1221(f) on 2026-10-09. Solar and storage: 300 ft from occupied community buildings and dwellings on nonparticipating properties, 50 ft from public road right-of-way and from nonparticipating property lines; solar panels max 25 ft at full tilt; wind: 2.1 times maximum blade tip height from occupied community buildings and nonparticipating residences; shadow flicker not more than 30 hours per year; 55 average hourly decibels (A-weighted) at the nearest dwelling on adjacent nonparticipating property for solar, wind and storage. 460.1221(f): compatible ordinance is no more restrictive than 226(8). Summary, who_decides, state_body, thresholds and citations match. History: Add. 2023, Act 233, Eff. Nov. 29, 2024; no later amendment.

summary: A commission site permit for a large energy infrastructure facility is the only site approval needed and supersedes and preempts all regional, county, local and special purpose government zoning, building and land use rules for the facility.
amendments_note: 216I.18 was renumbered from 216E.10 by 2024 Minn. Laws c. 126 art. 7 s. 14 and c. 127 art. 43 s. 14 (216E.10 subds. 1 to 3 also amended by 2024 c. 126 art. 9 ss. 8 to 10 and c. 127 art. 45 ss. 8 to 10), effective July 1, 2025. The former wind preemption section, 216F.07, was repealed (2024 c. 126 art. 7 s. 15; 2024 c. 127 art. 43 s. 15), not renumbered; wind is now covered because a large wind energy conversion system is a large energy infrastructure facility under 216I.02 subd. 10. No 2025 or 2026 amendment to 216I.18 shown on revisor.mn.gov as of 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Corrects the 2026-10-09 draft after review: amendments_note no longer says 216F.07 was renumbered into 216I.18; the revisor's 216F.07 page reads 'Repealed, 2024 c 126 art 7 s 15; 2024 c 127 art 43 s 15', and the 216E.10 page reads 'Renumbered 216I.18'. I agree with the reviewer. Added 216I.02 subd. 10 to the citation since it brings wind and storage into the preemption. Read 2026-10-09 on revisor.mn.gov: 216I.18 subd. 1 ('the sole site or route approval required to be obtained by the permittee. The permit supersedes and preempts all zoning, building, or land use rules, regulations, or ordinances promulgated by regional, county, local and special purpose government'), 216I.02 subds. 6, 9, 10, 11, 18, and the 216E.10 and 216F.07 status pages. Projects approved locally under 216I.08 get no commission permit, so this preemption does not reach them.
review_note: Read 2026-10-09 https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/216I.18 subd. 1: issuance of a site or route permit 'is the sole site or route approval required to be obtained by the permittee. The permit supersedes and preempts all zoning, building, or land use rules, regulations, or ordinances promulgated by regional, county, local and special purpose government.' 216I.02 subd. 10 (large energy infrastructure facility includes a large electric power generating plant, an energy storage system and a LWECS) with subds. 6, 9, 11, 18 gives the 10, 50, 5 and 50 MW figures, so threshold_mw solar:50;wind:5;battery_storage:10 matches. Summary, who_decides state_board, state_body and citation match. Amendments: 216I.18 history ends 2024 c 126 art 7 s 14, art 9 s 8-10; 2024 c 127 art 43 s 14, art 45 s 8-10, effective July 1, 2025 per the chapter note; the 216E.10 page reads 'Renumbered 216I.18'; the 216F.07 page reads 'Repealed 2024 c 127 art 43 s 15' and '2024 c 126 art 7 s 15'. The 216I.18 page shows no 2025 or 2026 amendment. Sabin record id not checked (a compiled source, not the statute).

summary: A large electric power generating plant may not be sited where its developed portion uses more than 0.5 acres of prime farmland per MW unless there is no feasible and prudent alternative; the rule does not apply inside or near cities.
amendments_note: Rule history 27 SR 1295; L 2005 c 97 art 3 s 19. Not among the chapter 7850 parts repealed by 2024 Minn. Laws c. 126 art. 7 s. 15 (that list skips 7850.4000 to 7850.4400 except 4100 and 4200). No later change shown on revisor.mn.gov as of 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Read Minn. R. 7850.4400 on revisor.mn.gov and the repealer in 2024 c. 126 art. 7 s. 15. Uncertain scope: the rule says "large electric power generating plant", and since 2024 216I.02 defines "solar energy generating system" separately from that term; the rule definitions part 7850.1000 was repealed. Wind (LWECS) is a separate category and its rule chapter 7854 was repealed, so I list solar only; Sabin lists wind and solar. The rule is a state rule, not a statute.
review_note: Read Minn. R. 7850.4400 at https://www.revisor.mn.gov/rules/7850.4400/ on 2026-10-09. Subp. 4: no large electric power generating plant site may be permitted where the developed portion includes more than 0.5 acres of prime farmland per megawatt of net generating capacity unless there is no feasible and prudent alternative; does not apply within home rule charter or statutory cities, within two miles of first, second and third class cities, or in orderly annexation areas (summary's inside or near cities is a fair short form). History 27 SR 1295; L 2005 c 97 art 3 s 19; no later change. Read the repealer 2024 c.126 art.7 s.15 subd. 4 (https://www.revisor.mn.gov/laws/2024/0/Session+Law/Chapter/126/): it repeals 7850.1000 to 7850.3900, 4100, 4200 and 4500 to 5600 but not 7850.4400, and repeals all of chapter 7854. who_decides and state_body match (the rule binds the commission). Technology: the rule names large electric power generating plants, not solar; solar is covered because Minn. Stat. 216I.02 subd. 9 defines that term as generating equipment of 50,000 kW or more, which a 50 MW solar system meets; the row's solar-only reading is an interpretation, as the draft note says, not words of the rule. threshold_mw blank is acceptable since the 50 MW figure comes from the statute, not the rule.

summary: The Public Utilities Commission issues site permits for solar and other generating plants of 50 MW or more, wind of 5 MW or more and storage of 10 MW or more; smaller projects need no commission permit but must still get any local, state or federal approval that applies and meet state environmental review rules. Applicants for solar and generating plants under 80 MW, wind under 25 MW and any storage system may instead seek local approval, unless a local unit of government asks the commission to take the case within 60 days.

Laws c. 126 art. 7 and c. 127 art. 43 created chapter 216I, effective July 1, 2025, renumbered 216E sections into it and repealed chapter 216F (including 216F.08, county assumption of wind permitting). Storage of 10 MW or more is now expressly covered. Neither changes the thresholds or who decides. The pages for 216I.02, 216I.03, 216I.08 and 216I.10 show no 2025 or 2026 amendment.

Read 2026-10-09 on revisor.mn.gov: 216I.02 (subd. 6 storage 10,000 kW; subd. 9 large generating plant 50,000 kW; subd. 11 LWECS 5,000 kW; subd. 18 solar 50,000 kW AC), 216I.03, 216I.06, 216I.07, 216I.08 subds. 1 and 2, 216I.10 subds. 1 and 2, 216F.07 and 216E.10 status pages.

summary: Missouri has no siting statute specific to wind or solar. By the statute's text, any electrical corporation (any person owning or operating an electric plant to sell power to others, other than municipal utilities and rural cooperatives) needs Public Service Commission approval before building an electric plant, except an energy generation unit of 1 MW or less, and cities and counties also regulate land use through their general zoning powers.
amendments_note: 393.170 last amended 2018 (S.B. 564); 386.020 last amended 2019 (H.B. 355); 89.020 last amended 2019 (S.B. 133); 64.620 L. 1951, A.L. 1991 H.B. 72; 64.850 L. 1965, A.L. 1974. Per revisor.mo.gov section histories, read 2026-10-09. The revisor's list of recently changed sections (revisor.mo.gov/main/recent.aspx, 2025 and 2026 effective dates) shows no new or amended section on solar or wind siting or decommissioning and no change to these sections; 2025 utility changes (for example 393.401 on plant closures and 393.1900 on resource planning) do not address siting. No section 67.5350 exists. 2026 SB 849 and SB 879 could not be checked (senate.mo.gov bill pages returned HTTP 404).
draft_note: Corrects the 2026-10-09 draft after review: who_decides changed from local_government to hybrid and state_body set to the Missouri Public Service Commission, because 393.170(1) requires commission approval before any 'electrical corporation' begins construction of an electric plant (other than an energy generation unit of one megawatt or less), and 386.020(15) defines electrical corporation as every corporation, company, partnership and person owning, operating, controlling or managing any electric plant, excluding only producers for their own use and not for sale to others, municipal utilities (ch. 91), rural electric cooperatives (ch. 394) and certain EV charging operators. Nothing in the text limits this to regulated utilities, so I agree with the reviewer and dropped 'only regulated electrical corporations'. Added 64.850 (first class non-charter and second to fourth class county zoning) because 64.620 covers only second and third class counties. Removed the unconfirmed news claim about SB 849 and SB 879. threshold_mw left blank: the 1 MW exemption is per energy generation unit, not a project-size threshold. summary: After January 1, 2026, a wind turbine built under a wind energy agreement that is 500 ft or taller to blade tip may not be placed within 1,500 ft of an occupied residence unless the property owner approves a shorter distance; such turbines near homes in icing areas must also mitigate ice throw.
statute_citation: Mont. Code Ann. sections 75-26-402, 75-26-403 (2025 Mont. Laws Ch. 761)
amendments_note: New after the inventory: enacted by 2025 Mont. Laws Ch. 761, sections 1 and 2; applies after January 1, 2026. No later amendment in MCA 2025 history as of 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Read 75-26-402 and 75-26-403 in MCA 2025 on leg.mt.gov. "Owner of the real property" is not further defined in the section; it is unclear whether it means the residence owner. Not in the inventory.
review_note: Read MCA 2025 75-26-402 (https://leg.mt.gov/bills/mca/title_0750/chapter_0260/part_0040/section_0020/0750-0260-0040-0020.html) and 75-26-403 on 2026-10-09. 402: after January 1, 2026, a wind turbine generator built pursuant to a wind energy agreement under 70-17-406 may not be constructed if 500 feet or more in height to blade tip and less than 1,500 feet from an occupied residence, unless a shorter setback is approved by the owner of the real property. 403: after January 1, 2026, turbines 500 feet or more, in an area with ice class rating 4 or more, within 1,500 feet of an occupied residence must use commercially reasonable efforts to mitigate icing risks during operator-controlled deicing. History: En. Secs. 1 and 2, Ch. 761, L. 2025; nothing later. Fields and citation match. Minor wording: 403 is not limited to turbines built under a wind energy agreement, while the summary's such turbines implies it is; and it addresses icing risk during deicing rather than ice throw generally.

summary: For plants that need Commission location approval, the Commission may declare a state, county or municipal land use regulation void as to the siting if it finds the regulation unreasonably restrictive and compliance not in the public interest; its judgment is conclusive on siting and local requirements.
amendments_note: Official history note not readable (HTTP 403). The 2025 edition text seen in search snippets matches; no 2024-2026 amendment found, not confirmed.

Ann. 62-9-3 in the official 2026 chapter 62 document (https://nmonesource.com/nmos/nmsa/en/4407/1/document.do) through Jina Reader on 2026-10-09 (direct curl HTTP 403). 62-9-3(G): an application may not be approved if it violates an existing state, county or municipal land use regulation 'unless the commission finds that the regulation is unreasonably restrictive and compliance with the regulation is not in the interest of the public convenience and necessity', in which case the regulation 'shall be inapplicable and void as to the siting'; the Commission must notify and may join the local land use body; 'The judgment of the commission shall be conclusive on all questions of siting, land use, aesthetics and any other state or local requirements affecting the siting.' summary: Local governments may not adopt rules that prohibit or unreasonably restrict a property owner from using a solar or wind energy system on the owner property, though reasonable wind rules on location, noise, safety and setback, and denials for safety or incompatibility, remain allowed.
amendments_note: 278.02077 last amended 2017; 278.0208 last amended 2009, per NRS chapter 278 (revised 9/9/2026, 2026R1) on leg.state.nv.us. None after the inventory.
draft_note: Read both sections. The wording ("owner of real property ... on his or her property") reads as aimed at owner-use systems, and I found no definition of "system for obtaining wind/solar energy" in chapter 278; reviewer should decide whether this reaches utility-scale facilities. 278.02077(2)(b) expressly lets a governing body deny a wind permit for safety or incompatibility with the area.
review_note: Read NRS 278.02077 and 278.0208 at https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nrs/NRS-278.html (Rev. 9/9/2026, 2026R1) on 2026-10-09. 278.02077: a governing body shall not adopt an ordinance, regulation or plan or take other action that prohibits or unreasonably restricts the owner of real property from using a system for obtaining wind energy on his or her property; subsection 2 allows reasonable restrictions from an FAA hazard determination or relating to finish, location, noise, safety or setback, and denial of a permit where size, height or configuration endangers public health, safety or welfare or is incompatible with the area. 278.0208: same prohibition for solar, with deemed-unreasonable restrictions (efficiency loss over 10 percent; ban on black solar glazing). Summary, blank who_decides, state_body and threshold, technology and citations match. Histories end 2017, 1298 and 2009, 1599 as the note says. summary: Renewable generating plants over 70 MW need a utility facility permit from the Public Utilities Commission, which may issue only if the location conforms to local law and the applicant has or is seeking local approvals; plants of 70 MW or less need only local and other approvals.

Laws ch. 56, part QQ per the Sabin row; not checked against the session law). nysenate.gov shows section 1005 revised 2024-05-03, 2024-05-24, 2024-12-27, 2025-01-10, 2025-02-21 and 2025-12-26 since 2023; the current 27-a(b) lead-in also covers projects under subdivision 27-b (the REACH bill-credit program), so 27-a(b) has been amended since 2023, but which revision added that wording was not identified (earlier revisions could not be displayed).
