state_body: Office of Renewable Energy Siting and Electric Transmission (ORES), Department of Public Service
summary: Renewable energy facilities of 25 MW or more, with any co-located storage, need an ORES siting permit under Public Service Law Article VIII; smaller facilities get no state siting permit and stay under municipal land use control. Battery storage that is not co-located with such a facility is outside the ORES rules.
statute_citation: N.Y. Pub. Serv. Law sections 137(4), 140(1) (Article VIII); 16 NYCRR 1100-1.1(d)(5), 1100-1.2(bb)
amendments_note: Superseded since the inventory: the inventory cites N.Y. Executive Law section 94-c; the program now sits in Public Service Law Article VIII (sections 136 to 148), whose pages on nysenate.gov show most recent revision 2024-06-21 (the 2024 RAPID Act; session-law chapter not confirmed from the statute pages) and a repeal date of December 31, 2040. ORES rules were replaced again: new 16 NYCRR Parts 1100 (general procedures), 1101 (major renewable energy facility siting) and 1102 (transmission) took effect March 9, 2026, replacing the Part 1100 of 2024-07-17 (dps.ny.gov/ores-regulatory-documents, read 2026-10-09). The new Part 1100 has no opt-in for facilities under 25 MW.
draft_note: Corrects the 2026-10-09 draft after review: removed 'facilities of 20 to 25 MW may opt in', since neither Pub. Serv. Law 137 nor 140 provides an opt-in and the March 9, 2026 Part 1100 has no opt-in definition; replaced the superseded rule citations (former 1100-1.1(b)(4)-(5), 1100-1.2(ag), (ba)) with the current 1100-1.2(bb) (major renewable energy facility, 25,000 kW or more with co-located storage) and 1100-1.1(d)(5) ('any battery energy storage system not co-located with a major renewable energy facility'); amendments_note now records the 2026-03-09 replacement rules. I confirmed each review point and agree. Read 2026-10-09: Pub. Serv. Law 137, 140 and the Article VIII section list via WebFetch of https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/PBS/137, /PBS/140 and /PBS/A8 (curl gets a Cloudflare challenge); 137(4) 'nameplate generating capacity of twenty-five thousand kilowatts or more, and any co-located system storing energy'; 140(1) 'No person shall commence the preparation of a site for, or begin the construction of, a major renewable energy facility ... without having first obtained a major renewable energy facility siting permit'. Rules read in full from https://dps.ny.gov/chapter-xi-title-16-nycrr-part-1100-general-procedures (PDF, 'Effective March 9, 2026'). The local half of hybrid is an inference: Article VIII gives no state permit below 25 MW, so local land use rules govern; no statute read says so in words.
review_note: Read 2026-10-09: N.Y. Pub. Serv. Law 137, 140, 142, 144, 162 and the Article VIII section list via Jina Reader (r.jina.ai) of https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/PBS/137, /140, /142, /144, /162 and /A8 (full statutory text returned; direct curl gets a Cloudflare challenge). 137(4): major renewable energy facility is a renewable energy system 'with a nameplate generating capacity of twenty-five thousand kilowatts or more, and any co-located system storing energy generated from such a renewable energy system'; 140(1): 'No person shall commence the preparation of a site for, or begin the construction of, a major renewable energy facility ... without having first obtained a major renewable energy facility siting permit'. No opt-in for smaller facilities appears in 137, 140 or 162 (162(4)(e) and (5) elections cover pending Article 10 facilities of 25 MW or more only). 144(2) bars local approvals only for facilities whose siting permit application has been filed, consistent with local control below 25 MW (an inference the summary states fairly). state_body: Office of Renewable Energy Siting and Electric Transmission (ORES), Department of Public Service
summary: ORES rules set uniform setbacks for facilities it permits: wind turbines 2 times total height from non-participating residences and 1.1 times from property lines and public roads; solar 250 feet from non-participating occupied residences and 100 feet from non-participating residential property lines, with arrays no taller than 20 feet. Noise outside non-participating homes is capped at 45 dBA Leq (2-hour) for wind and 45 dBA Leq (1-hour) for solar.
amendments_note: 16 NYCRR Part 1101, effective March 9, 2026, replaced the siting standards in the former Part 1100 (effective 2024-07-17), which had replaced 19 NYCRR Part 900 (dps.ny.gov/ores-regulatory-documents, read 2026-10-09). Comparing the two texts read 2026-10-09: the main setbacks (wind 2 times and 1.1 times total height; solar 250 feet and 100 feet) and the 20-foot solar height limit are unchanged; the noise limits changed from 45 dBA Leq (8-hour) at non-participating residences for both wind and solar (former 1100-2.8(b)) to 2-hour for wind and 1-hour for solar.
draft_note: Corrects the 2026-10-09 draft after review: citations and statute_url moved from the superseded 2024 Part 1100 (1100-2.6(b), (d), 1100-2.8(b)) to the current Part 1101 effective March 9, 2026; the noise limit is now 45 dBA Leq (2-hour) outside non-participating type 1 sensitive sound receptors for wind (1101-3.5(a)(1)(i)) and 45 dBA Leq (1-hour) for solar (1101-2.7(b)(2)), not 45 dBA Leq (8-hour); amendments_note records the 2026 replacement. I confirmed each review point in the rule text and agree. Added the 20-foot solar height limit in 1101-2.5(e). Read 2026-10-09 the Part 1101 PDF at statute_url ('Effective March 9, 2026') and, for comparison, the former Part 1100 PDF (https://dps.ny.gov/system/files/documents/2024/08/chapter-xi-title-16-of-nycrr-part-1100-generation-siting-effective-2024-07-17.pdf). Table 5-1 also: substations and above-ground bulk electric system 1.5 times, non-participating non-residential structures 1.5 times, gas wells 1.1 times; manufacturer setbacks apply if stricter. Table 5-2 also: 50 feet from the centerline of public roads, 25 feet from the public road right of way, 50 feet from non-participating non-residential property lines. Noise also: 55 dBA at participating type 1 receptors, 40 dBA Leq (1-hour) from collector substation equipment, 55 dBA Leq (1-hour) across non-participating type 2 receptors. These are uniform standards and conditions written into each ORES permit (1100-9.1(a)); they apply only to facilities ORES permits (25 MW or more), not to smaller projects under local rules.
review_note: Read 2026-10-09 the 16 NYCRR Part 1101 PDF at statute_url ('Effective March 9, 2026'). 1101-2.5(b) Table 5-1: wind turbine setback 2 times total height from non-participating residences, 1.1 times from public roads and property lines (1.0 times equals total height at maximum blade tip). 1101-2.5(d) Table 5-2: solar 100 feet from non-participating residential property lines and 250 feet from non-participating occupied residences. 1101-2.5(e): solar facilities no taller than twenty feet from finished grade. 1101-2.7(b)(2): solar 45 dBA Leq (1-hour) outside any non-participating type 1 sensitive sound receptor; 1101-3.5(a)(1)(i): wind 45 dBA Leq (2-hour) outside non-participating type 1 receptors; 1101-2.7(h)(1)(i) defines type 1 receptors to include residences, so 'outside non-participating homes' is accurate. threshold_mw solar:25;wind:25 follows from Part 1100 1100-1.2(bb) (25,000 kW), read in the Part 1100 PDF. who_decides state_board and state_body correct. Amendments: compared with the former Part 1100 effective 2024-07-17 (https://dps.ny.gov/system/files/documents/2024/08/chapter-xi-title-16-of-nycrr-part-1100-generation-siting-effective-2024-07-17.pdf): 1100-2.6 Tables 1 and 2 had the same 2x, 1.1x, 250 foot and 100 foot setbacks and the same 20 foot height limit; 1100-2.8(b) set 45 dBA Leq (8-hour) for both wind and solar. The note's description of the 2026 change is correct.

summary: A board of county commissioners may designate all or part of the county's unincorporated area as a restricted area that bars large solar facilities and wind farms of 5 MW or more, and the Power Siting Board may not accept applications there; the county may also prohibit or shrink an individual project within 90 days after the developer's required public meeting.

review_note: Read on codes.ohio.gov 2026-10-09: sections 303.57, 303.58, 303.59, 303.60, 303.61, 303.62, 4906.021 and 4906.022 (https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-303.58 and the matching pages). 303.58(A): the board of county commissioners may designate all or part of the unincorporated area as a restricted area prohibiting economically significant wind farms (5 to under 50 MW), large wind farms and large solar facilities (50 MW or more). 303.60: no person may file and the Power Siting Board may not accept an application in a restricted area. 303.61: developer public meeting 90 to 300 days before applying. 303.62: within 90 days after that meeting the county may prohibit the facility or limit its boundaries; with no resolution the application proceeds. 303.59 adds a referendum on petition by 8 percent of the county gubernatorial vote. review_note: Read on codes.ohio.gov 2026-10-09: sections 4906.01, 4906.10, 4906.13, 4906.20, 303.213 and 519.213 (https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-4906.01 and the matching section pages). 4906.01(B)(1)(a): major utility facility is a generating plant of 'fifty megawatts or more'; (G) and (H) define large solar facility and large wind farm as such plants. 4906.13(A): economically significant wind farm is 'five or more megawatts but less than fifty megawatts'; 4906.20(A) requires a Board certificate for it. 303.213 and 519.213: county and township zoning covers small wind farms (outside Board jurisdiction) and small solar facilities under 50 MW. SB 52 county powers are in 303.57 to 303.62 (read for OH-local_opt_out-1). Thresholds solar:50, wind:5 and hybrid match. Nothing later shown.

summary: Turbines in Board-certificated wind farms must be at least 1.1 times total height from the wind farm property line and at least 1,125 feet from the blade tip to the nearest adjacent property line, unless all adjacent owners waive it.
amendments_note: Both sections last amended by 2014 Ohio HB 483 (130th GA), eff. 2014-09-15; no later version on codes.ohio.gov as of 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Read 4906.20 and 4906.201 on codes.ohio.gov. 4906.201 applies the same setback to wind plants of 50 MW or more. Applications found compliant before 2013-09-29 keep a 750-foot distance. The statute directs the Board to set this minimum by rule (Ohio Adm. Code chapter 4906-4, not read).
review_note: Read https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-4906.20 and section-4906.201 on 2026-10-09. 4906.20(B)(2)(a): Board rules must set a minimum turbine setback of 1.1 times total height (base to tip of highest blade) from the wind farm property line and at least 1,125 feet from the tip of the nearest blade at ninety degrees to the property line of the nearest adjacent property; (c): applies unless all adjacent owners waive it, or the Board requires more; (b)(i) keeps 750 feet for applications found compliant before 2013-09-29. 4906.201 applies the same setback to wind plants of 50 MW or more. Summary, wind:5 threshold and state_board match. Both sections show only the HB 483 (130th GA) version eff. 2014-09-15; no later version as of 2026-10-09.

summary: Oklahoma has no state siting permit for wind or solar; the Corporation Commission takes notices and reports and enforces statutory wind setbacks, while any land use approval comes from county or municipal zoning where it exists.
statute_citation: Okla. Stat. tit. 17, §§ 160.11-160.23 (Oklahoma Wind Energy Development Act)
amendments_note: 160.21 has a 2023 version (SB 782, Laws 2023, c. 126, § 22). 2025-2026 wind setback bills HB 2751 (failed in Senate Energy committee) and SB 2 (failed on House reading) were not enacted per oklegislature.gov bill pages checked 2026-10-09. Title 17 PDF compiled 2025-12-31.
draft_note: Read the official Title 17 compilation PDF from oklegislature.gov (OSCN DeliverDocument pages return a Cloudflare Turnstile challenge and WebFetch got HTTP 403). 160.21 requires notice to the Commission and county commissioners and a public meeting; 160.22 lets the Commission adopt rules and fees; no section requires a state siting approval. County zoning statutes (Okla. Stat. tit. 19, § 863.x, cited by the inventory) not read.
review_note: Read the official Title 17 compilation PDF https://oklegislature.gov/OK_Statutes/CompleteTitles/os17.pdf (created 2025-12-31) on 2026-10-09: the Oklahoma Wind Energy Development Act, 160.11 to 160.23, in full. 160.21 (both versions; v2 is SB 782, Laws 2023, c. 126, s. 22) requires notice of intent to the Corporation Commission, copies to county commissioners and municipalities, newspaper publication and a public meeting before construction; 160.20 sets setbacks the Commission enforces through attestations and penalties; 160.22 gives rulemaking and fee authority. No section requires a state siting approval. Title 17 also has only a Commercial Solar Facility Decommissioning Act (820 et seq.) for solar, which is a lease decommissioning law, not a siting permit. Summary, technology and local_government fit. The statement that land use approval comes from county or municipal zoning rests on the absence of a state permit; the county zoning statutes (tit. 19) were not read by me either. Amendments: oklegislature.gov bill pages checked 2026-10-09 show HB 2751 'Failed in Committee - Energy' and SB 2 'Third Reading, Measure failed: Ayes 44 Nays 49' and, in 2026, 'Fourth Reading, Measure failed: Ayes 20 Nays 67'; neither was enacted.

summary: No wind energy facility tower may be built within 1.5 nautical miles of a public-use or municipal airport runway centerline, a public school or a hospital; separately, each turbine needing an FAA Form 7460-1 needs an FAA no-hazard determination and Defense Department clearance before construction.
amendments_note: History note: added Laws 2015, c. 92; amended Laws 2017, c. 45; Laws 2018, c. 4; Laws 2019, c. 310 (HB 2118, emerg. eff. 2019-05-07); Laws 2023, c. 126, § 21 (eff. 2023-11-01). No 2025-2026 change (HB 2751 and SB 2 not enacted).
draft_note: Read 160.20 in the Title 17 PDF (compiled 2025-12-31) and the enrolled HB 2118 (2019) PDF at https://www.oklegislature.gov/cf_pdf/2019-20%20ENR/hB/HB2118%20ENR.PDF. The distance is nautical miles, measured from the tower base; it applies after 2015-08-21. Subsection C (military clearance) is a clearance requirement, not a distance setback. Disputes go to district court; Commission penalty up to $1,500 per day for failing to file the no-hazard documents.
review_note: Read Okla. Stat. tit. 17, 160.20 in https://oklegislature.gov/OK_Statutes/CompleteTitles/os17.pdf (created 2025-12-31) on 2026-10-09. 160.20(A): after 2015-08-21 no wind energy facility may be built with any tower base less than 1 1/2 nautical miles from the runway centerline of a public-use airport or a municipally owned airport, from a public school in a public school district, or from a hospital. (C): each turbine or structure needing an FAA Form 7460-1 needs an active FAA Determination of No Hazard and resolution of Defense Department impacts documented by the Clearinghouse before construction. (D): penalty up to $1,500 per day. Summary, technology and state body match. History note matches the amendments_note: added Laws 2015, c. 92; amended 2017 c. 45, 2018 c. 4, 2019 c. 310, 2023 c. 126, s. 21 (eff. 2023-11-01). The 2025-2026 setback bills HB 2751 and SB 2 failed per their oklegislature.gov bill pages (SB 2 also failed a 2026 fourth reading, 20 to 67).

summary: A Council site certificate binds all counties and cities as to site approval, and they must then issue the permits it addresses without further hearings; the Council may also find land use compliance despite unmet local criteria by taking a goal exception.
amendments_note: 469.401 history ends with 2025 c.305. 469.504 amended by 2026 Or. Laws c.46 (HB 4076), which adds a goal-exception finding for facilities using an existing plant's surplus interconnection.
draft_note: Read 469.401 in ORS chapter 469 (2025 edition) and the enrolled 2026 HB 4076. 469.401(5) keeps local authority over matters not in the certificate (building codes, fees).
review_note: Read ORS 469.401 and 469.504 in https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/ors/ors469.html (2025 edition) and enrolled 2026 HB 4076 (https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2026R1/Downloads/MeasureDocument/HB4076/Enrolled) on 2026-10-09. 469.401(3): a signed site certificate 'shall bind the state and all counties and cities and political subdivisions in this state as to the approval of the site', and they must issue the permits it addresses 'without hearings or other proceedings'. 469.504(1)(b) and (2): the Council may find goal compliance where the facility does not meet local substantive criteria, including by taking a goal exception. 469.401(5) keeps local authority over matters outside the certificate. Summary, state body and wind:300 (from 469.300(4) and (12)(a)(K)) match. Amendments confirmed: 469.401 history ends 2025 c.305; the 2026 table lists 469.504 amended by 2026 c.46 (HB 4076), which renumbers 469.504(2) into (2)(a) and adds (2)(b) deeming the exception standard met for a facility using an existing facility's surplus interconnection with no new transmission more than two miles out. That does not change the row; the citation 469.504(2) still points to the exception power.

summary: State land use rules cap solar PV on farmland that counties approve without a goal exception at 12 acres of high-value farmland, 20 acres of arable land and 320 acres of nonarable land, with a larger alternative path in eastern Oregon.
amendments_note: Rule history on the Secretary of State site: LCDD 5-2019 (eff. 2019-05-30, the rule Sabin describes), then LCDD 4-2021, LCDD 14-2024 (eff. 2025-01-01), LCDD 6-2025 (eff. 2026-01-01) and LCDD 10-2026 (eff. 2026-10-01). Section (44) lets eastern Oregon counties allow up to 160 acres on qualifying high-value farmland, 1,280 acres on arable land and 1,920 acres on non-arable land.
draft_note: Read the current rule text at secure.sos.state.or.us (2026-10-09). This is an administrative rule, not a statute (authority ORS 197.040). Larger projects need a Goal 3 exception under OAR 660-004 or a county program under OAR 660-023-0195. Sabin's '20 acres of other farmland' is the arable-land cap; nonarable land is 320 acres. The '86 percent of the Willamette Valley' figure is not in the rule.
review_note: Read OAR 660-033-0130 at https://secure.sos.state.or.us/oard/view.action?ruleNumber=660-033-0130 on 2026-10-09 (current text, history through LCDD 10-2026, effective 2026-10-01). (38)(g): solar PV on high-value farmland may not use more than 12 acres; (38)(i): arable land 20 acres; (38)(j): nonarable land 320 acres; (38)(k): an exception under ORS 197.732 and OAR 660 division 4 is needed to exceed them. (44): eastern Oregon counties may instead use (44)(b) to (n), with caps of 160 acres on qualifying high-value farmland, 1,280 acres on arable land and 1,920 acres on non-arable land ((44)(d)), or a program under OAR 660-023-0195. Summary, technology, local_government and state body (LCDC adopts the rule) match. One nuance the summary leaves out: (38)(h)(H) lets a facility exceed 12 acres on certain non-irrigated high-value farmland in a utility RPS service area without an exception. History matches the amendments_note for the period after June 2024 (LCDD 14-2024 eff. 2025-01-01, LCDD 6-2025 eff. 2026-01-01, LCDD 10-2026 eff. 2026-10-01); the note skips the 2020 amendments (LCDD 2-2020 to 15-2020), which predate the inventory and do not affect the row.

summary: The Energy Facility Siting Council certificates wind plants of 100 MW average capacity or more (300 MW peak under the 3.00 wind factor), solar thermal plants of 25 MW or more, and solar PV using more than 240, 2,560 or 3,840 acres depending on land class; counties handle smaller projects unless the developer or county elects state review.
amendments_note: The inventory's thresholds are out of date. 469.300 history: 2023 c.336; 2024 c.25 (HB 4015, battery storage); 2025 c.162 (HB 3874) raised the wind threshold from 50 to 100 MW average. Solar PV acreage is now 240/2,560/3,840 (inventory: 160/1,280/1,920). 2026 Or. Laws c.12 (HB 4031, eff. 91 days after 2026 sine die) amends 469.320 to exempt solar, wind, geothermal and marine facilities from the site certificate if local land use approval is applied for by 2028-12-31 and the project meets federal tax credit begin-construction and in-service conditions.
draft_note: Read ORS chapter 469 (2025 edition, oregonlegislature.gov), Oregon Laws 2025 c.162 and 2024 c.25 PDFs, enrolled 2026 HB 4031 (olis.oregonlegislature.gov) and the 2026 A&R table (469.320 by c.12; 469.504 by c.46). Threshold_mw shows 300 for wind because the statute counts 'average electric generating capacity' of 100 MW and 469.300(4) divides wind peak capacity by 3.00. Solar PV uses acreage, not MW, so it is not in threshold_mw. Battery storage is a related facility or an elective item under 469.320(8)(a)(C), not a stand-alone energy facility.
review_note: Read ORS chapter 469, 2025 edition, at https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/ors/ors469.html on 2026-10-09, plus Oregon Laws 2025 c.162 (https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/lawsstatutes/2025orLaw0162.pdf), the 2026 amended-and-repealed table (https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/lawsstatutes/2026OrLawAR.pdf) and enrolled 2026 HB 4031 (https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2026R1/Downloads/MeasureDocument/HB4031/Enrolled). 469.300(12)(a)(K): wind plant with 'average electric generating capacity of 100 megawatts or more'; 469.300(4): wind average capacity is peak divided by 3.00, so wind:300 MW peak is the right conversion. (12)(a)(A)(iii): solar thermal at 25 MW nominal. (12)(a)(D): solar PV using more than 240 acres of high-value farmland, 2,560 acres of cultivated or class I to IV land, or 3,840 acres of other land. 469.320(1) requires a site certificate; 469.320(8) lets the developer or the local government elect Council review for smaller wind, solar PV and battery storage. Summary, threshold and hybrid match. Amendments confirmed: 469.300 history ends 2023 c.336, 2024 c.25, 2025 c.162; c.162 struck wind from the 50 MW average clause and added the 100 MW wind clause. The 2026 table lists 469.320 amended by 2026 c.12 (HB 4031) and 469.300 not amended in 2026. HB 4031 adds 469.320(2)(h): solar, wind, geothermal or marine facilities need no site certificate if the developer applies for local land use approval by 2028-12-31 and receives it, notifies the local government and the Council that construction has begun for a federal 45, 45Y, 48 or 48E credit, and places the facility in service by 2030-12-31 (or a later date Treasury allows); effective the 91st day after the 2026 session adjourned, so in force now. The amendments_note describes this correctly; the drafter may want the summary itself to say that qualifying large projects can now go to the county instead.

summary: Pennsylvania has no state siting permit for wind or solar; municipalities (and counties where a municipality has no zoning) regulate them through zoning under the Municipalities Planning Code.
statute_citation: Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code, Act of July 31, 1968, P.L. 805, No. 247, §§ 601, 602, 619 (53 P.S. §§ 10601, 10602, 10619)
amendments_note: The current compiled MPC on palegis.us shows a 2024 amendment (Act 44 of 2024, electronic transmittal, section 110) unrelated to energy siting; no 2024-2026 state wind or solar siting law found.
draft_note: Read the MPC PDF from palegis.us. Section 619 lets the PUC exempt a public utility corporation's buildings from zoning after a hearing; independent generators are not usually public utilities, so not drafted as preemption. No state statute names wind or solar siting.
review_note: Read the compiled Municipalities Planning Code PDF from palegis.us (https://www.palegis.us/statutes/unconsolidated/law-information/view-statute?txtType=PDF&SessYr=1968&ActNum=0247.&SessInd=0, linked from the statute_url page) on 2026-10-09. Section 601: each municipality's governing body may enact zoning ordinances; section 602: county zoning applies only in municipalities with no zoning ordinance in effect; section 619: the Public Utility Commission may exempt a public utility corporation's building from the zoning article after a hearing. The Code names solar and wind only as planning purposes, not as a state permit. Summary, technology and local_government fit; the 'no state siting permit' statement is an absence I could not disprove. Amendments: the compiled text shows section 110 added by Act 44 of 2024 (July 8, 2024, electronic transmittals), unrelated to siting. The state siting board bill HB 502 of 2025 (RESET Board) shows last action 'Referred to Energy, April 23, 2025' on https://www.palegis.us/legislation/bills/2025/hb502, so it is not law.

state_body: Oficina de Gerencia de Permisos (OGPe), Department of Economic Development and Commerce
summary: Puerto Rico's general permit law, which does not mention renewable projects, has the central Permit Management Office (OGPe) and its adjudicative board issue construction and land use permits and siting decisions, except that autonomous municipalities holding a delegation of hierarchy levels I to V have exclusive authority over the permits covered by their delegation agreements.
statute_citation: Puerto Rico Act 161-2009 (Ley para la Reforma del Proceso de Permisos), arts. 1.3, 2.1, 2.5, 18.10 (23 L.P.R.A. sections 9011 note, 9012, 9012d, 9024i)
amendments_note: OGPe's compiled text is marked 'Rev. 14 de mayo de 2026'. Its list of amending laws adds, since June 2024, Laws 61-2024, 118-2024, 119-2024, 122-2024, 124-2024, 131-2024, 106-2025, 111-2025 and 82-2026. Notes in the text tie 61-2024, 118-2024, 124-2024, 131-2024, 106-2025 and 111-2025 to arts. 2.7A, 3.4, 8.4B, 9.11, 19.12 and other articles; none is noted on arts. 1.3, 2.1, 2.5 or 18.10. The compilation shows no article note for Laws 119-2024, 122-2024 or 82-2026, so what they changed was not identified.
draft_note: Corrects the 2026-10-09 draft after review: who_decides changed from state_board to hybrid, because art. 1.3 gives autonomous municipalities with a delegation of hierarchies I to V 'total exclusividad para otorgar determinaciones finales y permisos, según establecido en su correspondiente convenio de delegación' (also art. 2.5 and art. 18.10), so permit authority is split between OGPe and those municipalities; the summary now says the Act does not mention renewable projects instead of 'including for renewable projects'; amendments_note lists the 2024 to 2026 amending laws. I agree with the reviewer, and found three amending laws in the compilation's list (119-2024, 122-2024, 82-2026) that the review did not name. Art. 2.5 also sends siting consultations of regional or supra-regional impact to OGPe or its Junta Adjudicativa, and rezonings to the Planning Board; art. 18.10 shows OGPe still decides applications from autonomous municipalities that fall outside their delegated hierarchy. Read 2026-10-09: the compiled Act 161-2009 PDF (Spanish) at statute_url, arts. 1.3, 2.1, 2.5, 18.10 and the amendment notes. Energy Bureau approvals under Acts 57-2014 and 17-2019 were not read.
review_note: Read 2026-10-09 the OGPe compilation of Act 161-2009 (Spanish, 106 pages, 'Rev. 14 de mayo de 2026') at statute_url. Art. 1.3 (23 L.P.R.A. 9011 nota): the Act applies to anyone seeking final determinations and permits for construction and land use; autonomous municipalities with a delegation of hierarchies I to V 'tendrán total exclusividad para otorgar determinaciones finales y permisos, según establecido en su correspondiente convenio de delegación'. Art. 2.1 (9012): OGPe created as an auxiliary secretariat of the Department of Economic Development and Commerce. Art. 2.5 (9012d): OGPe issues final determinations and permits, autonomous municipalities with hierarchies I to V may issue them under arts. 1.3 and 18.10, and OGPe or the Junta Adjudicativa decides use variances, construction and siting consultations including those of regional or supra-regional impact; rezonings go to the Planning Board. Art. 18.10 (9024i): delegated municipalities; OGPe adjudicates their applications outside the delegated hierarchy. A text search finds no use of 'renovable', so 'does not mention renewable projects' is accurate. who_decides hybrid, state_body, blank threshold, summary and citations match. Amendments: the compilation's list adds Laws 61-2024, 118-2024, 119-2024, 122-2024, 124-2024, 131-2024, 106-2025, 111-2025 and 82-2026; article notes tie 61-2024 to art. 8.4B, 118-2024 to art. 3.4, 124-2024 to art. 2.7A, 131-2024 and 111-2025 to the article at 23 L.P.R.A. 9018c, 106-2025 to arts. 8.16 and 9.11, and 111-2025 also to art. 19.12 (supremacy over conflicting laws); none is noted on arts. 1.3, 2.1, 2.5 or 18.10, and no article note names 119-2024, 122-2024 or 82-2026, as the row says. Energy Bureau laws (Acts 57-2014, 17-2019) were not read.

summary: For major energy facilities the Siting Board is the licensing authority for every permit or variance that state law or local ordinance would require; local boards hear the matter but only send findings and a recommendation to the Siting Board.
amendments_note: History ends with P.L. 1994, ch. 14; none shown as of 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Read 42-98-7 on webserver.rilegislature.gov. DEM keeps federally delegated permits and CRMC keeps its coastal permits (42-98-7(a)(3)).
review_note: Read https://webserver.rilegislature.gov/Statutes/TITLE42/42-98/42-98-7.htm on 2026-10-09. 42-98-7(a)(1) makes the Siting Board the licensing and permitting authority for every license, permit, assent or variance required by state statute or local ordinance; (a)(2) has the agencies and local boards that would otherwise decide 'sit and function at the direction of the siting board', follow their own procedures, and forward findings, the record and a recommendation to the Board instead of issuing the permit. (a)(3) keeps federally delegated DEM permits and DEM and CRMC permits with those agencies (the draft note says so). Summary, state body and the 40 MW threshold (42-98-3(e)) match. History ends with P.L. 1994, ch. 14; no change after June 2024 seen.

summary: Distributed generation projects in core forests (unbroken forest blocks of 250 acres or more) cannot take part in the Renewable Energy Growth program, and net-metering systems must be sited outside core forests, unless they are on a preferred site such as a landfill, brownfield, parking lot or rooftop (net metering also exempts projects already in the permit or interconnection process on April 15, 2023); on preferred sites in a core forest no more than 100,000 square feet of core forest may be cleared, and new net-metering projects cannot be split across adjoining core-forest parcels except on preferred sites.
amendments_note: Core forest provisions enacted by P.L. 2023, ch. 300 and ch. 301 (2023-S 0684A, 2023-H 5853A), eff. 2023-06-24. 39-26.6-3 history ends P.L. 2024, ch. 83 and ch. 84, eff. 2024-06-12. 39-26.4-2 and 39-26.4-3 histories end P.L. 2025, ch. 256 (S 0843) and ch. 269 (H 5580), both eff. 2025-06-27; I read both acts on webserver.rilegislature.gov: they change excess net-metering credit pricing (now the ISO-New England energy clearing price), rules for systems of 25 kW or less, cash-out of credit balances and a 2050 date to 2060, and restate the core forest provisions without change. As shown 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Corrects the 2026-10-09 draft after review: the summary now follows 39-26.4-2(19) ('Subject to the safe-harbor provisions in 39-26.4-3(a)(1), new and distinct projects cannot be located on adjoining parcels of land within core forests, except for preferred sites') instead of saying such projects 'are not treated as distinct'; amendments_note now names P.L. 2025, ch. 256 and ch. 269, which I read. I agree with the reviewer. Also changed: I found that 39-26.4-3(a)(1)(ii) states the net-metering rule directly ('Eligible net-metering systems shall be sited outside of core forests with the exception of development on preferred sites in the core forest' and systems that had applied for permits or interconnection by April 15, 2023), so it is now cited and summarized; the 300 MW figure in 39-26.6-12(c) is an annual program target (with 30 MW reserved for projects under 1 MW), not a cap on siting, so it was dropped from the summary. Read 2026-10-09 on webserver.rilegislature.gov: 39-26.6-3, 39-26.6-12, 39-26.4-2, 39-26.4-3 and PublicLaws/law25/law25256.htm and law25269.htm. These are incentive and net-metering eligibility conditions, not a ban: a core forest project can still be built without Renewable Energy Growth or net-metering benefits. Distributed generation under 39-26.6-3(7) is up to 5 MW (solar up to 15 MW, or 39 MW on preferred sites).
review_note: Read 2026-10-09 on webserver.rilegislature.gov: R.I. Gen. Laws 39-26.6-3, 39-26.4-2, 39-26.4-3 and PublicLaws law25/law25256.htm, law25269.htm, law23/law23300.htm, law23301.htm. 39-26.6-3(6): core forest is unfragmented forest blocks of 250 acres or more, and no renewable distributed generation project in a core forest is eligible for the program unless on a preferred site; (7): distributed generation up to 5 MW (solar up to 15 MW, or 39 MW on preferred sites) and for facilities in core forests on preferred sites no more than 100,000 sq. ft. of core forest removed (except interconnection or brownfield work); (15): preferred sites include landfills, brownfields, parking lots and all rooftops. 39-26.4-2(2) same core forest definition; (19): 'Subject to the safe-harbor provisions in 39-26.4-3(a)(1), new and distinct projects cannot be located on adjoining parcels of land within core forests, except for preferred sites' (the summary's 'cannot be split across adjoining core-forest parcels' is a fair paraphrase). 39-26.4-3(a)(1)(ii): net-metering systems sited outside core forests except preferred sites and systems that by April 15, 2023 had applied for municipal permits or zoning, requested a paid interconnection study, or completed a paid interconnection application; (iii): the 100,000 sq. ft. cap. Summary, blank who_decides, state_body and threshold, policy_type other and citations match. Amendments: 39-26.6-3 history ends P.L. 2024 ch. 83 and 84, eff. June 12, 2024; 39-26.4-2 and -3 end P.L. 2025 ch. 256 and ch. 269, eff. June 27, 2025. I extracted the struck and underlined text of both 2025 acts: changes cover systems of 25 kW or less, excess credit pricing, credit cash-out and 2050 to 2060; none touches core forest, preferred site or adjoining-parcel wording. P.L. 2023 ch. 300 is H 5853 Sub A and ch. 301 is S 0684 Sub A, both enacted 06/24/2023, consistent with the note. Sabin record ids not checked.

summary: Generating facilities of 40 MW or more are major energy facilities licensed by the Energy Facility Siting Board; smaller facilities are regulated by city and town zoning.
amendments_note: None since the inventory: history notes on webserver.rilegislature.gov end with P.L. 2001, ch. 145 (42-98-3) and P.L. 1994, ch. 14 (42-98-7), as of 2026-10-09.
draft_note: Read 42-98-3 and 42-98-7 on webserver.rilegislature.gov. The inventory cites 42-98-3(d) for the threshold; the definition is now subsection (e). Storage is not named.
review_note: Read on webserver.rilegislature.gov 2026-10-09: https://webserver.rilegislature.gov/Statutes/TITLE42/42-98/42-98-3.htm, .../42-98-7.htm and the chapter 42-98 index. 42-98-3(e): major energy facility includes 'facilities for the generation of electricity designed or capable of operating at a gross capacity of forty megawatts (40 MW) or more' (the definition is now subsection (e), as the draft says). 42-98-7(a)(1): the Siting Board is the licensing and permitting authority for all licenses, permits, assents or variances that state law or local ordinance would require for siting a major energy facility. Thresholds solar:40 and wind:40, state body and hybrid (Board at 40 MW and above, local zoning below) match; storage not named. History notes end with P.L. 2001, ch. 145 (42-98-3) and P.L. 1994, ch. 14 (42-98-7); the chapter index shows no new section, so no change after June 2024 seen.

summary: No state body sites wind or solar in Alabama; local governments decide. Local acts give Baldwin County zoning power over wind facilities and require a local permit for any commercial wind system in Cherokee, DeKalb and Etowah counties; a utility building a plant also needs a certificate of convenience and necessity from the Public Service Commission.
amendments_note: History notes on alison.legislature.state.al.us as of 2026-10-09: 45-2-262 Act 2013-440; 45-10-260.02 Act 2014-190; 45-25-260.02 Acts 2015-348 and 2015-387; 45-28-260.02 Act 2014-191; 37-4-28 Code 1940; no later amendment shown. 2026 bills for a one-year statewide solar moratorium (HB617, SB354, SB372), county solar zoning (HB618, SB358) and solar permits and decommissioning (HB623) show no act number on the legislature site, so none was enacted.
draft_note: Read the sections through the Code of Alabama on alison.legislature.state.al.us (the site loads text from its public GraphQL endpoint, alison.legislature.state.al.us/graphql). A full-text search of the code for solar energy, solar facility and photovoltaic found no siting statute for solar. 37-4-28 is the PSC certificate for utility plants, not a siting permit for merchant generators; drafted local_government as LBNL does.
review_note: Read on alison.legislature.state.al.us (Code of Alabama, text served by alison.legislature.state.al.us/graphql, the endpoint the code page uses): 45-2-262 (Baldwin County commission zoning power over wind facilities, Act 2013-440), 45-10-260.02, 45-25-260.02 and 45-28-260.02 (unlawful to build or operate a wind energy conversion system in Cherokee, DeKalb or Etowah County without a permit from a local governing body; 260.01 limits the term to systems built for resale), and 37-4-28 (PSC certificate of convenience and necessity before a plant for production of electricity is constructed; Code 1940). A full-text search of the code on the same site for solar, solar energy, solar facility and photovoltaic found only tax credit, state land leasing and definition sections, and for wind energy only these local acts, 11-106 and the PSC jurisdiction sections 260.08; no state siting permit. who_decides local_government, blank state_body and threshold, technology and citations match. Amendments: history notes match the row and show no change after June 2024. The 2026 bills HB617, SB354, SB372 (one-year solar moratorium), HB618, SB358 (county solar zoning) and HB623 (solar permits and decommissioning) have no act number in the site's bill data (SB354 passed the Senate only; SB358 indefinitely postponed), so none was enacted.

summary: In Cherokee, DeKalb and Etowah counties only, state law requires every commercial wind energy conversion system to sit at least 2,500 feet from the nearest edge of any adjacent property, keep noise at its own property line at or below 40 decibels, and set back 1.5 times tower height from overhead power lines, with financial assurance including $1,000,000 for damage to adjoining property.
draft_note: Read the three sections on alison.legislature.state.al.us. These are local acts codified in Title 45 that apply to three named counties, not statewide; drafted as state_setback_standard because the standard is set by state statute, but the reviewer may prefer other. Laws in Order cites only the permit sections (260.02) and does not mention the setback or noise limits. Wind systems are defined as those built for resale of the energy.
review_note: Read 45-10-260.01, -260.02, -260.04, -260.05 and the DeKalb (45-25-) and Etowah (45-28-) counterparts on alison.legislature.state.al.us (graphql endpoint). The numbers in the summary match the text: 40 decibels at the system's property line (260.05(i)), 2,500 feet from the center-mass base to the nearest edge of the adjacent property (260.05(j)), 1.5 times tower height from overhead power lines (260.05(k)), and $1,000,000 financial assurance for damage to adjoining property (260.04(b)); history notes (Acts 2014-190, 2014-191, 2015-348 and 2015-387) show no amendment after June 2024. Field wrong: policy_type. The row says state_setback_standard, a type defined in the drafting brief as a statewide standard; these are local acts in Title 45 that apply only in Cherokee, DeKalb and Etowah counties (each section is in a county's part of Title 45 and the permit duty in 260.02 is limited to that county). The row should use a type that does not claim a statewide standard (for example other), with the summary keeping the three-county limit.

summary: Statewide, a wind energy facility may not encroach on or adversely affect military operations and readiness, and a local government may not approve one until the developer shows a Department of Defense Siting Clearinghouse finding of no presumed risk, a mitigation agreement, or an FAA determination of no hazard (or the approval is conditioned on one); notice to the Clearinghouse is due at least 270 days before construction.
amendments_note: 11-106-6 history: Act 2021-114 s2; Act 2025-139 s1. Act 2025-139 (2025 SB 91) amended 11-106-3, -4 and -6 to require local approval for tall structures within 2 miles of a military installation and drop a minimum acreage from the definition of military installation; the wind provisions read here are the current text.
draft_note: Read 11-106-3, -4, -5 and -6 on alison.legislature.state.al.us and the Act 2025-139 summary from the legislature instrument record. Not in Laws in Order. A siting precondition rather than a ban; drafted as other.
review_note: Read 11-106-3, 11-106-4 and 11-106-6 on alison.legislature.state.al.us (graphql endpoint). 11-106-6(a) bars any wind energy facility in the state from encroaching on or adversely affecting military operations and readiness; (e) requires the documentation, including notice to the DoD Siting Clearinghouse, at least 270 days before planned construction; (f) bars local approval before a Clearinghouse no presumed risk finding, a mitigation agreement, or an FAA Determination of No Hazard; (g) allows approval conditioned on one of them. 11-106-3(8) defines wind energy facility; 11-106-4(b) ties local approval to 11-106-6. Summary, technology, policy_type other, who_decides local_government and citations match. Amendments: history shows Act 2021-114 and Act 2025-139; the current text includes the 2025 tall structure two-mile approval in 11-106-6(b) and a military installation definition with no acreage minimum, consistent with the note; the wind provisions read are current. No later act shown.

summary: Boroughs and cities with planning powers regulate land use, including permits that encourage or discourage specified uses; no state body issues a siting permit for wind or solar. A wind or solar plant that sells power to the public needs a certificate of public convenience and necessity from the Regulatory Commission of Alaska, but renewable plants up to 65 MW placed in service before July 1, 2028 that sell only to regulated utilities are exempt.
amendments_note: The akleg.gov statutes are the 2025 edition and carry no history notes. The July 1, 2028 date in 42.05.711(r) was set by 2021 SB 69 (ch. 13 SLA 2021), per web search results pointing to akleg.gov/pdf/billfiles/SLAs/sl21pdfs/CH013.pdf (not opened). A web search found no 2025 or 2026 Alaska statute on wind or solar siting.
draft_note: Read 29.40.040, 42.05.221, 42.05.990 and 42.05.711 in print view on akleg.gov (Alaska Statutes 2025). Laws in Order calls Alaska Both because of the RCA certificate; I drafted local_government because 42.05.221 certifies a utility to provide service rather than approving a plant site, and 42.05.711(r) exempts many independent renewable plants. Reviewer may prefer hybrid. Much of Alaska lies in the unorganized borough, which has no borough land use regulation; this row does not address state land leasing.
review_note: Read AS 29.40.040, 42.05.221, 42.05.990(6) and 42.05.711 in print view on akleg.gov (https://www.akleg.gov/basis/statutes.asp?media=print&secStart=<section>&secEnd=<section>, Alaska Statutes 2025, all HTTP 200). 29.40.040 has the assembly adopt zoning and land use permit rules, including permits designed to encourage or discourage specified uses. 42.05.221(a) bars a public utility from operating and receiving compensation without an RCA certificate of public convenience and necessity; it certifies a utility's service and area, not a plant site, so who_decides local_government with blank state_body is a fair reading against Laws in Order's Both, and I accept it. Field wrong: summary. It says renewable plants up to 65 MW placed in service before July 1, 2028 that sell only to regulated utilities are exempt. 42.05.711(r) also requires that the plant be first placed in commercial operation on or after August 31, 2010 and that its owner or operator has not received a state grant used to generate the electricity or a state tax credit related to that generation; without the grant and tax credit condition the summary states the exemption more broadly than the statute. Amendments: akleg.gov statute pages carry no history notes; a web search (2026-10-09) found only the 2021 SB 69 (ch. 13 SLA 2021) setting the July 1, 2028 date and no 2025 or 2026 act changing these sections.

summary: Counties, cities and towns decide siting of wind and solar photovoltaic projects through zoning. The state Power Plant and Transmission Line Siting Committee issues certificates of environmental compatibility only for thermal, nuclear or hydroelectric units of 100 MW or more, a definition that names no wind or photovoltaic technology; where a certificate is needed, the committee may override a local rule it finds unreasonably restrictive.
amendments_note: azleg.gov section pages show no history notes. The 2025 and 2026 bills that would have added county rules for wind and solar (2025 SB 1150 House engrossed version; 2026 HB 2337 and HB 2338, which would have added 11-820.05) show no chapter number in the azleg.gov bill API as of 2026-10-09, and 11-820.05 on azleg.gov is an unrelated assisted living section. The similar 2023 HB 2618 was vetoed.
draft_note: Read 40-360, 40-360.03 and 40-360.06 on azleg.gov. Laws in Order treats solar thermal plants of 100 MW or more as needing a state certificate because they are thermal electric units; the statute does not say so expressly, so I left threshold_mw blank and drafted local_government for photovoltaic and wind. Reviewer may prefer hybrid with solar:100 limited to solar thermal. Battery storage not addressed in the statute.
review_note: Read ARS 40-360, 40-360.03 and 40-360.06 on azleg.gov (https://www.azleg.gov/ars/40/00360.htm, 00360-03.htm, 00360-06.htm; HTTP 200, 2026-10-09). 40-360(9) defines plant as a thermal electric, nuclear or hydroelectric generating unit of 100 MW or more; 40-360.03(A) requires a utility (40-360(11): any person generating electric energy) planning a plant or transmission line to apply for a certificate of environmental compatibility, referred to the siting committee; 40-360.06(D) conditions certificates on local ordinances unless the committee finds compliance unreasonably restrictive and not feasible in view of available technology. On the drafter's question: local_government with blank threshold stands for wind and photovoltaic solar, since the plant definition names neither; a solar thermal unit of 100 MW or more would fall under thermal electric, and the summary correctly confines the local statement to photovoltaic. Summary, technology, policy_type and citations match. Amendments: azleg.gov section pages carry no history notes. In the azleg.gov bill API (apps.azleg.gov/api/Bill), 2026 HB 2337 (zoning; use permits), 2026 HB 2338 (board; votes; wind; solar projects) and 2025 SB 1150 show no chapter number and no governor action, so none was enacted; no change to the row through 2026-10-09 found.

summary: Since 2025 a wind energy facility of 5 MW or more that is over 200 feet tall needs a permit from the Public Service Commission and also a local permit wherever the local government has adopted wind legislation. Solar is decided locally, except that a utility generating plant of 50 MW or more needs a certificate of environmental compatibility and public need from the Commission, which exempt wholesale generators do not need.
amendments_note: Act 945 of 2025 (SB 437) approved 2025-04-21; per the Sabin 2026 report it took effect 2025-08-03, and per an Arkansas Attorney General opinion (2026-024) summary it is codified at 23-18-1401 to -1419. It exempts facilities under development as of 2025-04-09 and facilities begun by 2024-09-01. The Commission adopted rules in Docket 25-063-R on 2026-01-14 (secondary sources say they await Legislative Council approval; not checked). A web search found no 2026 fiscal session bill amending the act. A rival 2025 wind bill, SB 639, died in House committee.
draft_note: Opened the enrolled Act 945 PDF on arkleg.state.ar.us (sections 23-18-1303, -1304, -1310, -1313, -1318). Not opened: Ark. Code 23-18-503, -504 and -510 on the utility facility certificate (the official code is on Lexis only; law.justia.com returned a Cloudflare challenge via curl, Jina and WebFetch HTTP 403; no Wayback capture found; Firecrawl out of credits, all 2026-10-09). Under Act 945 the local permit applies only where local legislation exists.
review_note: Wind part opened and matches: read the enrolled Act 945 of 2025 (SB 437, approved 4/21/25) on arkleg.state.ar.us (https://arkleg.state.ar.us/Acts/FTPDocument?path=%2FACTS%2F2025R%2FPublic%2F&file=945.pdf&ddBienniumSession=2025%2F2025R, HTTP 200). Act sec. 23-18-1303(17) defines wind energy facility as 5 MW or more and more than 200 feet; 23-18-1304(a)(2) requires a Public Service Commission permit and, where the local government has adopted wind legislation, a local permit; 23-18-1310(c) and 23-18-1318 give the 2024-09-01 and 2025-04-09 exemptions. Codification: Act 940 of 2025 (SB 596, also approved 4/21/25, with an emergency clause; enrolled PDF 940.pdf on arkleg.state.ar.us) also created Ark. Code Title 23, Ch. 18, Subchapter 13 as 23-18-1301 to -1303, so Act 945 could not keep those numbers; the text of Attorney General Opinion 2026-024 (April 22, 2026, as reproduced on ezel.ai via r.jina.ai; arkansasag.gov not opened) says Act 945 is now codified at 23-18-1401 to -1419 and cites 23-18-1413 for local permits, so the row's 1401 numbering is supported. Web search snippets (openei.org RAPID 8-AR-c and 8-AR-d) give the 50 MW figure only secondhand, and an Arkansas Supreme Court opinion snippet reads the act as reaching only public utility facilities, which bears on the exempt wholesale generator wording and needs checking against the code. Also in amendments_note: the row gives an effective date of 2025-08-03 (attributed to Sabin); Act 945 has no emergency clause, and search results for Attorney General Opinion 2025-032 give August 5, 2025 as the effective date of such 2025 acts (opinion not opened), so the drafter should recheck that date.

summary: To get a state permit, each turbine must sit at least the greater of 3.5 times its tip height or 2,500 feet from a nonparticipating property line (waivable to 1.1 times height) and one mile from schools, hospitals, nursing homes, churches, city or town limits, state or federal parks and public airports; noise may not exceed 35 dBA at a nonparticipating dwelling or 45 dBA at the property line, and shadow flicker is capped at 30 hours a year. Local wind rules may be stricter but not less restrictive.
amendments_note: New in 2025 (Act 945, approved 2025-04-21), after the June 2024 inventory. A web search found no later amendment as of 2026-10-09; the codified text on Lexis was not read.
draft_note: Read 23-18-1306 and 23-18-1313 in the enrolled Act 945 PDF on arkleg.state.ar.us. Applies to wind energy facilities of 5 MW or more and over 200 feet. The Sabin row gives only the dwelling noise limit; the act also sets 45 dBA at the property line and adds city limits, parks and airports to the one-mile list. The codified section numbers (-1406, -1413) assume the 1301 to 1401 renumbering reported in the AG opinion summary.
review_note: Read the enrolled Act 945 of 2025 on arkleg.state.ar.us (https://arkleg.state.ar.us/Acts/FTPDocument?path=%2FACTS%2F2025R%2FPublic%2F&file=945.pdf&ddBienniumSession=2025%2F2025R). Act sec. 23-18-1306(a)(1): setback from a nonparticipating landowner's property line the greater of 3.5 times total tip height or 2,500 feet, waivable by the landowner to 1.1 times tip height; (a)(2): one mile from schools, hospitals, nursing homes, churches, the limits of a city or town, state or federal parks and public airports; (b)(2)(B)(vi)(b): shadow flicker not over 30 hours a year (waivable under (c)); (c)(1): 35 dBA at a nonparticipating dwelling and 45 dBA at the property line (weather exception and landowner waiver in (c)(3)). 23-18-1313(a)(2): local legislation may not set permit criteria less restrictive than the subchapter. Applies to wind energy facilities of 5 MW or more and over 200 feet (23-18-1303(17)), so threshold wind:5, technology, who_decides state_board and the PSC as state_body match. Codified numbers -1406 and -1413: Act 940 of 2025 (enrolled PDF on arkleg.state.ar.us) separately created 23-18-1301 to -1303, and the text of AG Opinion 2026-024 (April 22, 2026, reproduced on ezel.ai) states Act 945 is codified at 23-18-1401 to -1419 and cites 23-18-1413, consistent with the row. Amendments: no 2026 fiscal session act amending the subchapter found in web search as of 2026-10-09; the codified text on Lexis was not read.

summary: Counties and cities decide most wind, solar and storage projects, but a developer of a photovoltaic or terrestrial wind plant of 50 MW or more, or a storage system of 200 MWh or more, may instead apply (until June 30, 2030) to the California Energy Commission, which then has exclusive power to certify the site. Thermal plants of 50 MW or more, including solar thermal, must be certified by the Commission; wind and photovoltaic plants are excluded from that mandatory track.
amendments_note: Section histories on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov as of 2026-10-09: 25545 amended by Stats. 2025, ch. 372 (AB 531), eff. 2026-01-01 (adds geothermal and other facility types); 25545.1 and 25545.2 amended by Stats. 2025, ch. 119 (SB 254), eff. 2025-09-19 (25545.1 now sets an application deadline of June 30, 2030); 25500 last amended 1976; 25120 last amended 1988. Per secondary sources, 2025 SB 283 (signed 2025-10-06, eff. 2026-01-01) applies NFPA 855 fire standards to storage certified under the opt-in program; not read. 2025 AB 303 (3,200-foot storage setback) did not pass.

summary: When a developer of an eligible wind, photovoltaic or storage project uses the Energy Commission opt-in process, the Commission certificate replaces local permits and supersedes local ordinances, including those of charter cities; the Coastal Commission, State Lands Commission and water boards keep their authority.
amendments_note: Amended by Stats. 2025, ch. 119 (SB 254), eff. 2025-09-19, per the section history on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov as of 2026-10-09; the supersession language in (b)(1) and the charter city clause in (c) are in the current text.
draft_note: Read 25545.1 on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov via Jina Reader. Preemption applies only if the developer opts in; it is not automatic. Storage eligibility is 200 MWh or more.
review_note: Read Pub. Res. Code 25545.1 and 25545 on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov through Jina Reader (https://r.jina.ai/https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PRC&sectionNum=25545.1, HTTP 200, 2026-10-09). 25545.1(b)(1): a certificate under the chapter is in lieu of any state, local or regional permit and supersedes any applicable local ordinance or regulation; (b)(2): does not supersede the State Lands Commission, Coastal Commission, BCDC, State Water Resources Control Board or regional water boards; (c): applies to all cities, including charter cities. Applies only where a person files an application under 25545.1(a), so the opt-in framing in the summary is right. Eligible wind and photovoltaic plants are 50 MW or more and storage 200 MWh or more (25545(b)), so threshold solar:50;wind:50, who_decides state_board, state_body, technology and citation match. Amendment: section history shows Stats. 2025, ch. 119 (SB 254), effective 2025-09-19; the supersession and charter city language is in the current text. No later amendment shown.

summary: Counties and municipalities decide siting of wind, solar and storage through their land use codes; the state gives them technical help and model codes but has no siting permit of its own. A public utility also needs a certificate of public convenience and necessity from the Public Utilities Commission, which by statute does not decide siting, and its new plants must comply with local zoning unless it wins an appeal under 29-20-108.
amendments_note: Source notes in Colorado Revised Statutes 2024 (official uncertified printout on content.leg.colorado.gov): 40-5-101 last amended L. 2012 (HB 12-1312); 29-20-401 to -405 added L. 2024 (SB 24-212), eff. 2024-05-21. The 2025 edition PDF returned HTTP 404 on 2026-10-09, so 2025 and 2026 changes were checked only by web search, which found no later amendment.
draft_note: Read 40-5-101 and 29-20-108 and Part 4 of Article 20 (29-20-401 to -405) in the CRS 2024 title PDFs. SB 24-212 (Renewable Energy Projects Act) requires local governments to consult the Ute Mountain Ute and Southern Ute tribes before permitting a wind, solar or storage facility in the Brunot area (29-20-405) and gives state technical support; it adds no state permit. Laws in Order calls Colorado Both; I drafted local_government because the PUC role is limited to utility projects (see CO-local_preemption-1). Reviewer may prefer hybrid.
review_note: Read C.R.S. 40-5-101 in Colorado Revised Statutes 2024, title 40 PDF (https://content.leg.colorado.gov/sites/default/files/images/olls/crs2024-title-40.pdf), and 29-20-108 and 29-20-401 to -405 in the title 29 PDF (crs2024-title-29.pdf), both HTTP 200 on 2026-10-09; the crs2025 title PDFs at the same path returned HTTP 404. 40-5-101(1)(a): a public utility needs a PUC certificate of public convenience and necessity, which does not include siting issues for transmission lines and associated facilities; 40-5-101(3): except as provided in 29-20-108, a utility's new facility must comply with local zoning, and nothing in (3) gives the PUC added authority to restrict a siting application. 29-20-403 to -405 (SB 24-212): definitions covering commercial wind, solar (5 MW AC) and storage facilities, state technical support and a code repository (404), and tribal consultation in the Brunot area (405); no state permit. On the drafter's question: local_government with blank state_body and threshold is a fair reading; the PUC certificate applies only to public utilities and is not a site approval, and the utility appeal is covered in CO-local_preemption-1. Summary, technology and citations match. Amendments: source notes match the row (40-5-101 last L. 2012, HB 12-1312; part 4 added L. 2024, SB 24-212, eff. May 21). For 2025 and 2026: the 2026 PUC sunset act HB26-1326 (signed 5/29/2026; final act PDF leg.colorado.gov/bill_files/116854/download) amends 40-5-106 but not 40-5-101 or article 20 of title 29; HB26-1278 (would have added 29-20-108(8)) is marked Lost on leg.colorado.gov. No change to the row found.

summary: For generating facilities proposed by a public utility or power authority, the local government must act within 90 days of a final application (120 days of a preliminary one) or the application is deemed approved, and the utility may appeal a denial or unreasonable conditions to the Public Utilities Commission, which balances local and statewide interests. Independent developers that are not utilities do not get this appeal.
amendments_note: 29-20-108 source note (CRS 2024): added L. 2000; (2),(4),(5) L. 2001; (2) amended L. 2005 and L. 2014 (HB 14-1129); (3) amended and (6) added L. 2022 (HB 22-1104); (7) added L. 2023 (SB 23-016). No 2025 or 2026 amendment found by web search; the 2025 edition was not available to check.
draft_note: Read 29-20-108 in the CRS 2024 title 29 PDF. Electrical generating facilities are major electrical facilities under 29-20-108(3)(a)(I). The statute covers public utilities and power authorities only.
review_note: Read C.R.S. 29-20-108 in Colorado Revised Statutes 2024, title 29 PDF (https://content.leg.colorado.gov/sites/default/files/images/olls/crs2024-title-29.pdf, HTTP 200) and 40-5-101(3) in the title 40 PDF. 29-20-108(2): final local action on a public utility or power authority application for major electrical facilities within 120 days of a preliminary application or 90 days of a final one, or the application is deemed approved; (3)(a)(I): electrical generating facilities are major electrical facilities; (5)(a): a utility or power authority may appeal a denial or conditions that unreasonably impair safe, reliable and economical service to the PUC; (5)(d): the PUC balances local and statewide interests. The section names only public utilities and power authorities, so the statement that independent developers do not get the appeal is supported. Summary, technology, who_decides state_board, state_body and blank threshold match. Amendments: the source note matches the row (through L. 2023, SB 23-016). 2026: a House Finance amendment to HB26-1326 would have extended the (5) appeal to independent power producers and others, but the final act as signed 5/29/2026 (leg.colorado.gov/bill_files/116854/download) contains no change to 29-20-108; HB26-1278 (would add 29-20-108(8)) is marked Lost. No change to the row found through 2026-10-09; the 2025 CRS edition PDF returned HTTP 404.

summary: The Connecticut Siting Council has exclusive jurisdiction over the location and type of electric generating and storage facilities; only renewable plants of 1 MW or less owned by a private power producer that is a federal qualifying facility (or built mainly for own use) fall outside it and are left to local zoning. Projects that may have a substantial adverse environmental effect need a certificate of environmental compatibility and public need, while distributed resource projects up to 65 MW are approved by declaratory ruling.
amendments_note: 16-50k amended by P.A. 25-127, eff. 2025-07-08 (decommissioning bond also for 2 MW or larger solar on prime farmland approved by declaratory ruling), per the 2026 Supplement on cga.ct.gov; 16-50i and 16-50x show no 2025 change (history notes end at P.A. 07-222 for 16-50x). A web search found no 2026 public act amending these sections.
